kjv-isaiah-block-quotation.responseLead: The King James wording came with the translation, not from the plates themselves.
kjv-isaiah-block-quotation.response:
FAIR and Skousen agree the translation was never word for word. Where the plates matched the Bible, the familiar King James wording was given. Two reasons are offered. Joseph may have consulted a Bible. Or, in Skousen's tight-control model, revelation supplied him with King James style English.

On that reading the King James wording is a feature of how the book was given. It is not evidence against an old source. Skousen goes further. He argues that some Isaiah variants come from Early Modern English streams of text. They are not copied from the 1611 page at all.
kjv-isaiah-block-quotation.rationaleLead: Strong for you: their own leading textual scholar grants where the English came from.
kjv-isaiah-block-quotation.rationale:
Their own leading textual scholar grants the core fact. The English text comes from the King James Bible. It even carries printing habits added after 1611. Skousen does not dispute that.

So the replies explain the dependence. They do not rebut it.

kjv-italics-revision.responseLead: Stan Spencer says Joseph saw the italics and revised the weakest words on purpose.
kjv-italics-revision.response:
Stan Spencer, of the Interpreter Foundation, accepts the pattern. He argues that Joseph Smith could see the italics on the page. An untrained reader would treat them as the weakest part of the verse. So Joseph revised around them as he dictated.

On that view a revealed translation would land on exactly those words. FAIR argues much the same. The italic words really were the softer text. A prophetic revision would be expected to correct there first.
kjv-italics-revision.rationaleLead: Strong for you: both sides now agree the changes cluster on 1611's added words.
kjv-italics-revision.rationale:
Both sides now agree on the fact. The changes cluster on the italics. Those are a printing feature of one English Bible from 1611. That is no longer in dispute.

What the defence offers is a reframe, not a denial. And the reframe grants the thing that matters. He was working from a King James Bible.

One problem is left over. In several places, dropping the italic word hurts the sense against the Hebrew. A revision guided by God would not be expected to do that.

kjv-translation-errors-copied.responseLead: The errors sit in the English translation layer, not on the ancient plates.
kjv-translation-errors-copied.response:
FAIR argues that a functional translation aimed at King James readers may keep familiar wording. That holds even where the wording is imperfect. Some of the alleged errors are also fair readings of Hebrew that is genuinely unclear.

There is a scriptural warrant too. D&C 1:24 has God speaking to people after the manner of their language. On that account the errors belong to the English layer. They do not belong to the plates.
kjv-translation-errors-copied.rationaleLead: Strong for you: the King James marks are granted, then moved somewhere else.
kjv-translation-errors-copied.rationale:
The King James marks are conceded. The defence moves them into a translation habit given by God. It does not show that the readings are anything but King James errors.

And one thing is missing. No variant anywhere pulls the wording back toward the Hebrew. If God were correcting the 1611 committee, you would expect that somewhere.

deutero-isaiah-problem.responseLead: Either the wording came in when it was turned into English, or the late dating is wrong.
deutero-isaiah-problem.response:
Two lines of answer, and they pull in opposite ways. Kevin Barney and FAIR accept the scholarly dating. They suggest the material entered during translation. Joseph rendered Nephite ideas in the King James Isaiah his readers knew.

Other defenders reject the dating instead. They argue for one author. Or they argue for an early core of Isaiah 40-55 that could have existed by 600 BC. They also note that late-dating Isaiah partly assumes prophecy cannot predict.
deutero-isaiah-problem.rationaleLead: Strong for you: both answers cost them a great deal, and one gives up the plates.
deutero-isaiah-problem.rationale:
The exile dating of Isaiah 40-55 is one of the firmest results in Hebrew Bible study. Trained Latter-day Saint scholars accept it, David Bokovoy among them.

So the defences have to pick. Reject the consensus, which is a large thing to do. Or accept it and move the material into the translation. That second route grants that the plates could not have held those chapters.

It costs a lot. Abinadi's whole sermon is built on Isaiah 53.

sermon-on-mount-3-nephi.responseLead: Welch shows one variant runs the other way, matching the earliest manuscripts against the King James.
sermon-on-mount-3-nephi.response:
John W. Welch of BYU responded at length. Several of Larson's eight variants are uncertain rather than settled. One runs the other way. 3 Nephi 12:22 leaves out 'without a cause', agreeing with the earliest manuscripts against the King James of Matthew 5:22.

Welch also argues that the King James wording elsewhere reflects the register of the translation. It does not reflect the Nephite record. And 3 Nephi adapts the sermon to its setting on purpose. Mechanical copying would not do that.
sermon-on-mount-3-nephi.rationaleLead: Arguable both ways: Welch's reverse case is real, but the added prayer line is not.
sermon-on-mount-3-nephi.rationale:
Welch's reply engages the variants seriously. The missing 'without a cause' at 3 Nephi 12:22 is a real point for them. Hand it over before anyone asks.

The prayer ending at 3 Nephi 13:13 and the word 'openly' are still best explained by King James dependence. Scholars do argue over single cases. The King James register across the whole sermon is not in doubt.

nt-phrasing-in-preexilic-books.responseLead: The New Testament wording came in with the English, for Bible readers of the 1820s.
nt-phrasing-in-preexilic-books.response:
FAIR and Frederick argue that the New Testament language belongs to the translation. It does not belong to the plates. Joseph Smith, or a revealed translation aimed at 1820s Bible readers, put Nephite ideas into the scriptural English his audience knew.

The King James New Testament itself renders ideas with shared covenant wording. Some parallels may also reflect common Old World sources. Others may reflect real parallel revelation of the same gospel to prophets before Christ.
nt-phrasing-in-preexilic-books.rationaleLead: Strong for you: BYU grants the 650 phrases, and the answer concedes the English is not literal.
nt-phrasing-in-preexilic-books.rationale:
The fact is granted even at BYU. Hundreds of distinctly New Testament phrases run through the text. Nicholas Frederick counts about 650.

The translation-idiom defence does not rebut that. It grants that the English text is not a literal rendering of an old record.

And it strains hardest where a New Testament passage gives a whole sermon its shape. Moroni 7 and Moroni 10 are the clearest cases.

hebrews-in-alma-12-13.responseLead: Both texts could draw on older Melchizedek lore, and the Dead Sea Scrolls hold some.
hebrews-in-alma-12-13.response:
John W. Welch and the FARMS reviewers argue that Alma 13 and Hebrews could draw on the same older material. Melchizedek traditions are attested in Second Temple texts. 11QMelchizedek and the Genesis Apocryphon are two of them.

The shared King James wording, they say, is translation register. And Alma's treatment pulls a different way from Hebrews. Alma is about repentance and ordination. Hebrews is about Christ's superiority. Plain copying would not predict that.
hebrews-in-alma-12-13.rationaleLead: Leans your way, but their older-source answer is real and not yet ruled out.
hebrews-in-alma-12-13.rationale:
Wright's word-by-word case is detailed. Nobody has taken it apart.

The shared-tradition reply is a real answer. But no manuscript holds the Alma 13 argument, so it stays a guess. And it does not simply grant that Alma leans on Hebrews.

The dispute is genuine. The parallels favour Wright. They do not close it.

mark-long-ending-mormon-9.responseLead: Some non-LDS scholars defend Mark's long ending, and the risen Lord could commission twice.
mark-long-ending-mormon-9.response:
Book of Mormon Central answers in KnoWhy 522, and gives two lines.

First, a minority of trained scholars outside the church defend the long ending as real. Nicholas Lunn and James Snapp argue that case from early church quotations and from the text itself.

Second, even if Mark 16:9-20 is a later addition, Moroni's source was the Nephite record of Christ's words. The King James phrasing is the register of the translation. The risen Lord could give the same charge in both hemispheres.
mark-long-ending-mormon-9.rationaleLead: Your case holds on the standard view, but their minority answer for Mark is real.
mark-long-ending-mormon-9.rationale:
The defence leans on a minority reading of the text. That reading does have published defenders outside the church. So whether Mark's long ending is original is genuinely disputed.

On the standard view, though, the problem stands. The risen Jesus in America quotes twelve verses that most scholars date to the second century.

horses-anachronism.responseLead: The word horse may be a borrowed label for a native beast, and bone rots fast.
horses-anachronism.response:
Book of Mormon Central and FAIR offer three lines.

The word 'horse' may be a loanshift. That is a familiar label placed on a native animal such as a deer or a tapir. Spaniards and native peoples did exactly that with animals they had not seen before.

Small pockets of horses may also have survived into Book of Mormon times unnoticed. Wade Miller has had candidate late-dated remains tested. And a blank record counts for little in the tropics, where bone rarely survives.
horses-anachronism.rationaleLead: Strong for you, but the loanshift answer is fair and belongs in your mouth first.
horses-anachronism.rationale: No verified pre-Columbian horse has ever been produced. Radiocarbon tests on candidate remains come back either Ice Age or after contact. The loanshift defence grants the core point. No actual horses were there. And the horses harnessed to chariots resist the tapir reading, because a chariot needs a draught animal. Michael Coe of Yale set the problem out in Dialogue in 1973.

steel-and-ferrous-metallurgy.responseLead: The Vered Jericho sword proves Old World steel, and 'steel' can mean any hard metal.
steel-and-ferrous-metallurgy.response:
On the Old World half the defence is strong. The Vered Jericho sword is carburised steel, dated about 620 BC, and held in the Israel Museum. So 'most precious steel' was real in Lehi's Jerusalem. That is a genuine vindication.

For the New World, FAIR makes three points. 'Steel' in King James English can mean any hardened metal, and the King James uses it for Hebrew bronze. Mesoamericans did work meteoric iron. And a small Nephite industry could have left little trace, with its wording a loanshift.
steel-and-ferrous-metallurgy.rationaleLead: Split it: the Old World half is answered, the iron in America is not.
steel-and-ferrous-metallurgy.rationale:
The Old World steel is genuinely answered by the Vered Jericho sword. Concede that half plainly.

The other half is not answered. A Nephite and Jaredite iron and steel industry in the Americas has no support in the ground at all. Michael Coe and Deanne Matheny have both pressed this.

The word-meaning defence grants that no real steel was there. Yet the text has people being taught to make it.

wheat-barley-silk.responseLead: Little barley was farmed here before Columbus, and wheat and silk may be borrowed labels.
wheat-barley-silk.response: Apologists point to little barley, Hordeum pusillum. It is now confirmed as a farmed grain in pre-Columbian North America. Nobody knew that in 1830. So barley is no longer a clean anachronism. FAIR defends wheat and silk as loanshifts. A familiar label could stand for a like native grain such as amaranth. It could also stand for fine local fibres, like kapok, and the wild-silk cloth attested in Mesoamerica.
wheat-barley-silk.rationaleLead: Arguable and lopsided: barley is a real win for them, Old World wheat is not.
wheat-barley-silk.rationale: The little-barley find gives their case real traction, even though the species has shifted. Wild-silk cloth is genuinely attested too. Hand both over. Old World wheat is still unattested anywhere. And the loanshift answer again grants that the named plant was absent. The dispute is real, but lopsided. Michael Coe set out the first form of the problem in Dialogue in 1973.

greek-names-timothy-lachoneus.responseLead: Greek soldiers served Egypt from the 600s BC, so Greek names could reach Lehi's world.
greek-names-timothy-lachoneus.response:
Hugh Nibley and Stephen Ricks argue that Greeks were already in Lehi's world. From the mid-600s BC, Ionian and Carian soldiers and traders served Egypt. They fought in the army of Necho II and worked across the Levant.

So a Greek name could reach Lehi's people, and more easily the Mulekites. There is a second line too. 'Timothy', 'Jonas' and 'Alpha and Omega' may be the translator's English stand-ins for Nephite names and sayings.
greek-names-timothy-lachoneus.rationaleLead: A small case, and the Greek trade history is real; Lachoneus still fits 1829 better.
greek-names-timothy-lachoneus.rationale:
The mercenary reply rests on real history. Greeks were in Egypt and the Levant in the 600s BC. And the stand-in reading works well for 'Alpha and Omega'.

Two things still fit an 1829 writer better. One is 'Lachoneus' as a personal name. The other is wording that matches Revelation exactly. Grant Palmer made that case.

Neither side has a decisive case here, and this is a small point.

church-bible-synagogue-terms.responseLead: Those first two words are the translator's own, and the Bible line sits in a prophecy.
church-bible-synagogue-terms.response:
FAIR responds that 'church' and 'synagogue' are the translator's English words for whatever gatherings the Nephites had. The King James is loose with 'church' in the same way.

Lee Levine, who studies synagogues, allows for shared worship before the exile, in settings such as the gate chambers.

And 'Bible' appears inside an open prophecy of the latter days. Naming a future thing is exactly the point of such a prophecy.
church-bible-synagogue-terms.rationaleLead: Weak on the first two words; 2 Nephi 29 is the only part worth pressing.
church-bible-synagogue-terms.rationale:
Take 'church' and 'synagogue' as words only. Any theory of translation handles them. Translators always use their own words for groups and buildings. So do not press those two.

That answer does sit oddly beside Skousen's tight-control evidence.

2 Nephi 29 is different. Its 'Bible' passage answers critics of the 1830s in their own words. That reads better as 1830s writing than as prophecy.

another-gospel-canon-closure.responseLead: The closing curse seals one scroll only, and the Galatians point assumes what it must prove.
another-gospel-canon-closure.response: Three replies, and the first two are strong. Revelation 22:18 warns against tampering with 'the words of the prophecy of this book'. That means Revelation itself. It was a standard closing curse on a single ancient scroll. Revelation was not even the last book written. And the same logic applied to Deuteronomy 4:2 would cancel everything after Deuteronomy. Many evangelical scholars agree. Second, the warning is about men adding to scripture. It is not about God speaking again. Third, Galatians 1:8 condemns a different gospel. Latter-day Saints hold that the Book of Mormon teaches the same Christ crucified. On their reading the argument assumes what it is trying to prove.
another-gospel-canon-closure.rationaleLead: Drop the canon half; the Galatians half holds, and it tests us too.
another-gospel-canon-closure.rationale:
The Revelation 22:18 version is the weakest form of this argument. Christians should stop using it. Most textual scholars agree the curse is scoped to Revelation, and the Deuteronomy comparison lands.

The Galatians 1:8 form survives that reply. But it settles nothing on its own. It turns on whether the gospel content actually matches. That sends you to the doctrinal cases, on grace and on exaltation.

Not a standalone argument. Not answered either.

grace-after-all-we-can-do.responseLead: Robinson and Uchtdorf read the verse as grace in spite of all we can do.
grace-after-all-we-can-do.response: Four replies. Stephen Robinson of BYU and Royal Skousen read 'after all we can do' as an old turn of phrase. It means in spite of all we can do. Grace saves despite our failure, not after our success. In 2015 Dieter Uchtdorf of the First Presidency preached that 'after' does not mean 'because'. Salvation is not earned by hitting a quota. Third, in context Nephi's point is that the law of Moses is dead and only grace saves. Fourth, John Welch reads the verse against the covenant framing of Mosiah 4.
grace-after-all-we-can-do.rationaleLead: A draw: their newer reading is fair, but Moroni 10:32 still sets a test first.
grace-after-all-we-can-do.rationale: The 'in spite of' reading is possible in English, and after Uchtdorf it is close to official. That genuinely narrows the gap. Christians who ignore it are arguing with a position the church no longer holds. Two things keep the criticism alive. The new reading is late. From Joseph Fielding Smith through Kimball and McConkie, the standard reading was conditional. And Moroni 10:32 sets a condition in its grammar that no idiom removes. Deny yourselves of all ungodliness, then is his grace sufficient. Neither side lands a knockout.

dark-skin-curse.responseLead: The mark may mean garments, and the church disavowed the racial reading in 2013.
dark-skin-curse.response:
Scripture Central and recent BYU work argue that 'skin of blackness' may be a figure of speech. Ethan Sproat and Gerrit Steenblik read it as garments and marks the Lamanites took on. On that reading the curse itself is being cut off from the Lord at 2 Nephi 5:20. The mark is a separate thing.

FAIR notes that the book itself condemns Nephite racism. Jacob 3:5-9 calls the Lamanites more righteous. In some scenes the two peoples cannot be told apart, which a stark skin difference would prevent.

The heading edits fixed 1981 study helps by Bruce R. McConkie, not the revealed text. And the 2013 Gospel Topics essay 'Race and the Priesthood' disavows the idea that dark skin marks God's disfavour.
dark-skin-curse.rationaleLead: Strong for you, but make it gently: the garment reading is recent, the old teaching plain.
dark-skin-curse.rationale:
The figure-of-speech and garment reading is a late development. It cuts against nearly two centuries of the church's own teaching. Brigham Young taught the plain reading. So did Spencer W. Kimball, who reported Lamanite converts growing lighter.

The text's own chain resists it too. Cursed because of iniquity, therefore a skin of blackness, so they would not be enticing. 3 Nephi 2:15 has the curse and the skin change together.

The 2013 disavowal grants the criticism against the plain sense. It does not refute it.

fortunate-fall.responseLead: Christians have long taught the happy fault, and Augustine wrote 'O felix culpa' himself.
fortunate-fall.response: The BYU Religious Studies Center places this doctrine inside the old Christian felix culpa tradition, the happy fault. Ambrose taught it. Augustine wrote 'O felix culpa'. The Easter Exsultet still sings it. On that tradition the fall makes room for a greater good, the Incarnation. So a fall inside God's plan is not foreign to Christian faith. Scripture Central adds that Lehi's point is structural. Mortal life, choice and the capacity for joy all need a world built on opposition. 2 Nephi 2:11 says exactly that. They also call the fall a transgression of a lesser law rather than sin in the fullest sense. Some Christian theologians draw the same line. And Eve is honoured here rather than blamed.
fortunate-fall.rationaleLead: Their happy fault point is real, but the Genesis 1:28 command still has no answer.
fortunate-fall.rationale: The felix culpa parallel is a genuine steelman. Christians have long held that God brings a greater good out of the fall. Concede that at once. It does not reach the claim actually made here. 2 Nephi 2 says the fall was needed for children to be born. Genesis 1:28 has God command 'be fruitful, and multiply' before the fall. The text also says Adam and Eve would have stayed in innocence, having no joy. So the old tradition celebrates rescue in spite of the fall. 2 Nephi 2 makes the fall itself necessary. That is a different claim, and Genesis 1:28 still has no strong published answer.

original-sin-infant-baptism.responseLead: The Bible never commands infant baptism, and Baptists land where Moroni does.
original-sin-infant-baptism.response: FAIR makes three points, and they land. First, the Bible never commands infant baptism and never shows one. Baptists and most evangelicals agree with Moroni's practical result. So this is not simply Bible against Book of Mormon. It tracks a fight among Christians. Second, treating original sin as inherited guilt comes from Augustine. Eastern Orthodoxy rejects inherited guilt and keeps only a fallen nature and death. Psalm 51:5 is David's poetry about how deep sin runs, not a rule about infant guilt. Third, Latter-day Saints teach that Christ's atonement covers Adam's fall for children with no conditions. Moroni 8:8 says the curse of Adam is taken from them in him. So children are redeemed, not merely innocent.
original-sin-infant-baptism.rationaleLead: Do not use the simple version, or you will be arguing against many Christians too.
original-sin-infant-baptism.rationale:
As a proof-text fight the critics overreach. Infant baptism is disputed among Bible-believing Christians. So is inherited guilt. The Latter-day Saint reply finds real allies for parts of its case.

What survives is narrower but real. Moroni 8 sends infant-baptisers to hell. That condemns nearly all Christians before the Reformation, with a harshness no Bible text allows.

And the chapter argues a fight that came after the Bible, inside a text set in fourth-century America. The fight is Pelagius against Augustine, plus revival preaching in the 1800s. That shades into a question about where the text came from.

trinitarian-monotheism-1830.responseLead: Read whole, the 1830 text does tell Father and Son apart, as the New Testament does.
trinitarian-monotheism-1830.response:
David Paulsen and Ari Bruening of BYU argue the 1830 text is not modalist when read whole. It does tell Father and Son apart. The Father's voice introduces the Son in 3 Nephi 11, and Christ prays to the Father.

So its 'one God' language describes a unity of distinct persons. That is no further from later teaching than the New Testament's own 'one God' texts are from Nicaea.

Mosiah 15 is explained by divine investiture. Christ acts as Father by creation and covenant, and as Son in the flesh. The First Presidency set that out in 1916. Brant Gardner adds that the modalist ring may come from the limits of translation language.
trinitarian-monotheism-1830.rationaleLead: Arguable on that one charge, but the 1830 book says nothing of the later teaching.
trinitarian-monotheism-1830.rationale:
The narrow charge of modalism is genuinely arguable. Critics do sometimes overstate it. Paulsen really does find Father and Son told apart in the text.

The broader point survives anyway. The Book of Mormon insists on one eternal God. It says nothing at all about many gods, about eternal progression, about God having a body, or about people becoming gods. Those doctrines define mature Mormonism, and the 1830 book is silent on every one.

The 1916 divine-investiture framing exists because the plain text does not teach the later doctrine.

1837-son-of-edits.responseLead: Joseph was free to make his own work clearer, and Mosiah 16:15 still reads that way.
1837-son-of-edits.response:
Three replies. FAIR says a translator may clarify his own work. Royal Skousen treats the change as clarifying rather than correcting. Christ is still called Eternal Father elsewhere in the book, at Mosiah 16:15. Other verses of that kind were left alone, which a systematic cover-up would not do.

Second, the phrase 'mother of God' drew Catholic-sounding objections from Alexander Campbell. Taking it out removed a stumbling block without changing doctrine.

Third, thousands of changes across the editions are simply typographical. These four are printed openly in Skousen's variant lists. Nothing was hidden.
1837-son-of-edits.rationaleLead: Arguable, but watch the timing: the four edits land as his teaching about God moved.
1837-son-of-edits.rationale:
Nobody disputes the facts. FAIR grants the four insertions and grants that Joseph Smith made them. Only the meaning is argued. The point that similar wording survives elsewhere is fair, and it does weaken a cover-up framing.

One thing is not explained well by any Latter-day Saint source. Why would a translation given by God need a fix about Christ? And why at exactly the verses a critic had attacked, in exactly the years his teaching about God was shifting?

As evidence of a text that changed with its author, this stands. As proof of wholesale rewriting, it overreaches.

jacob-polygamy-vs-dc132.responseLead: Jacob 2:30 is an exception clause, and 2 Samuel 12:8 says God gave David those wives.
jacob-polygamy-vs-dc132.response:
FAIR reads Jacob 2:30 as an exception clause. Monogamy is the rule. But 'if I will, saith the Lord of Hosts, raise up seed unto me, I will command my people.' On that reading D&C 132 is the commanded exception, and the two texts state one policy.

On David and Solomon they draw a line. Jacob condemns the excess that was never authorised, the Bathsheba affair and the foreign wives who brought their idols. D&C 132:38-39 says David sinned only in the case of Uriah.

So the wives 'given of me' were the authorised ones. And 2 Samuel 12:8 does have Nathan say God gave David his master's wives.
jacob-polygamy-vs-dc132.rationaleLead: It is narrowed, not removed, and the strain shows the moment you reach Solomon.
jacob-polygamy-vs-dc132.rationale:
The harmony is available in the text. 2 Samuel 12:8 really does say that. And Jacob 2:30 can be read as an exception, though some scholars, Latter-day Saints among them, argue its grammar means the opposite.

The strain shows at Solomon. No text anywhere authorises Solomon's wives. Jacob condemns them and so does 1 Kings 11. Yet D&C 132:38 lists Solomon among those who sinned not.

The rule-plus-exception reading keeps the texts formally consistent. The price is that an 'abominable' practice becomes something God can grant. Narrowed, not removed.

unchangeable-god-vs-king-follett.responseLead: That verse is about God's character, not his past, and the ones around it fit that.
unchangeable-god-vs-king-follett.response:
Three replies. Blake Ostler and FAIR argue that Moroni 8:18 is about God's moral character. He is not partial or fickle. It is not about his history. The verses around it concern God's fairness to children, so reading a claim about his being into it is proof-texting.

Second, 'from all eternity to all eternity' can be a Hebrew way of saying throughout all the ages of this creation. That fits a being who always existed and was exalted before this creation began.

Third, since attaining godhood he is unchanging in everything that bears on salvation. That is all Mormon 9 needs for its argument about miracles.
unchangeable-god-vs-king-follett.rationaleLead: Strong for you: the Book of Mormon here sides with the Bible against later Mormon teaching.
unchangeable-god-vs-king-follett.rationale:
The character-only reading is hard to sustain. Moroni 8:18 and Mormon 9:9 use the language of time and being. It is the same formula the Bible uses of God in Psalm 90:2.

The Book of Mormon nowhere hints that God was once a mortal man. And the King Follett sermon frames the 1844 teaching as overturning the older view. That older view is exactly what the 1829 text holds.

The idiom-and-cycles reply is speculative and comes after the fact. No Latter-day Saint scripture supports it. Here the Book of Mormon sides with the Bible against later Mormonism, and that has not been answered.

no-postmortem-repentance.responseLead: Alma 34 warns those who had the gospel and threw it away, not those who never heard.
no-postmortem-repentance.response:
Three replies. Amulek is addressing the Zoramites, people who had the gospel and turned it down. His warning applies to them, not to the billions who never heard. D&C 138:32-34 limits acceptance after death to 'those who died without a knowledge of this gospel'. So the two texts divide humanity with no overlap.

Second, Latter-day Saints teach that character carries over after death. So this is no easy second chance, and Amulek's urgency still stands.

Third, 1 Peter 3:19 and 4:6 have Christ preaching to spirits in prison. 1 Corinthians 15:29 mentions baptism for the dead. So the later doctrine has biblical footing.
no-postmortem-repentance.rationaleLead: Their reading of Alma 34 is what the church teaches, but his words are sweeping.
no-postmortem-repentance.rationale:
The audience answer is coherent, and it is the church's actual teaching. Critics who ignore it are overclaiming.

It does strain the text. Amulek's words are universal in form. This life is the time for men to prepare. This is the final state of the wicked. The Book of Mormon repeats that scheme elsewhere without the carve-out.

And the whole apparatus of spirit prison, proxy ordinances and three degrees of glory is missing from a book whose next life is simply heaven or hell. As evidence of doctrine growing between 1829 and Nauvoo it holds. As a flat contradiction it can be answered.

born-at-jerusalem.responseLead: The verse says the land, not the city, and Amarna letter EA 287 uses it the same way.
born-at-jerusalem.response:
Three replies, and this is one of the better sets. The verse says 'at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers'. Land, not city. The Book of Mormon uses 'land of Jerusalem' more than forty times for the whole region Lehi left. Its writers were six centuries and an ocean away from Judean village geography.

Second, that phrasing is genuinely ancient. Amarna letter EA 287, from the fourteenth century BC, speaks of towns of the land of Jerusalem. A Dead Sea Scroll fragment says Jeremiah was taken captive from the land of Jerusalem. Neither was knowable in 1829.

Third, Bethlehem is five miles away, well inside any such land.
born-at-jerusalem.rationaleLead: One of their strongest replies: say so plainly, and do not lead with this case.
born-at-jerusalem.rationale:
This is among the strongest Latter-day Saint replies in the whole section, and Christians should say so plainly. The verse's own wording, the steady land-versus-city usage, and the genuinely ancient parallels give it real footing.

The counters keep some bite. The parallels are regional usages in other settings. And a nineteenth-century writer being loose explains the same data. Neither side closes it.

Note too that even on the critical reading this is an imprecision, not a clash of doctrine. That is why it is graded low.

plain-precious-things-removed.responseLead: If it happened before our oldest copies, then no copy we have could ever show it.
plain-precious-things-removed.response: Three replies. Scripture Central and FAIR move the loss earlier, into the first and second centuries. That is before our earliest substantial manuscripts, since most complete New Testament codices are fourth century. If it happened then, uniform later copies cannot rule it out. They cite Bart Ehrman on early changes made for doctrinal reasons. Second, the loss need not be deletion at all. 1 Nephi 13 mentions covenants as well as plain and precious things. So it could mean lost books the Bible itself names, or lost ordinances, or lost keys to reading. Third, the Dead Sea Scrolls show real fluidity in copying. Jeremiah and Samuel survive there in variant editions.
plain-precious-things-removed.rationaleLead: Strong for you on the popular version, but their retreat cannot be tested at all.
plain-precious-things-removed.rationale:
The manuscripts settle the popular form of this claim. There was no purge of doctrines out of the Bible after the apostles. The Dead Sea Scrolls close the Old Testament gap. The Great Isaiah Scroll, copied about 125 BC, matches the medieval Hebrew text about 95 percent word for word.

New Testament copying is too early, too spread out and too widely attested for a coordinated cut to leave no trace.

The careful version survives. But it survives only by retreating to where evidence is thinnest, and by becoming untestable. It also gives up the natural reading of 1 Nephi 13, and puts nothing positive in its place.

no-nephite-material-culture.responseLead: Sorenson's 500-mile map, and the NHM altars in Yemen sit right on Lehi's route.
no-nephite-material-culture.response:
Five replies, and one is a genuine hit.

John Sorenson's limited-geography model keeps the story inside a corridor of about 500 miles in Mesoamerica. On that model a hemisphere-wide blank is beside the point. He lists over 400 claimed matches.

Second, identifying a site may be impossible in principle. Only Maya script can be read with confidence, and the conquest erased most old place-names. Third, John Clark counts about 60 concrete things the text asserts. He reckons support for them rose from 13% in 1842 to 75% by 2005.

Fourth, and this is the strong one, the NHM altars from Yemen date to the seventh or sixth century BC. They sit on the right bearing for Lehi's route. Fifth, FAIR notes the famous Smithsonian statement was a form letter to cut down mail, not a research finding.
no-nephite-material-culture.rationaleLead: Strong for you: NHM is in Arabia, and says nothing about the New World two-thirds.
no-nephite-material-culture.rationale:
The reply explains why no signpost says Zarahemla. It does not answer the harder version. The text asserts a literate people with Old World crops, metalwork and writing. No remains of that kind exist anywhere in the Americas, and finding them would not require reading a place-name.

Clark's tally is generic. Warfare, thrones and cities are true of almost any complex society. NHM is a real hit, but it is in Arabia, where the story overlaps documented geography. It says nothing about the two-thirds of the book set in the New World.

And the small map is a retreat from the hemispheric reading Joseph Smith and every nineteenth-century leader held.

no-semitic-inscriptions.responseLead: Reformed Egyptian is the book's own phrase, and Stubbs claims 1,500 matches in Uto-Aztecan.
no-semitic-inscriptions.response:
Three replies. First, 'reformed Egyptian' is the text's own phrase for its script, 'altered by us, according to our manner of speech', at Mormon 9:32. It is not a claim that Egyptologists should know the name. Egyptian really was reformed over time, from hieroglyphic to hieratic to demotic. Hugh Nibley noted real cases of Semitic languages written in Egyptian characters.

Second, the record was a small elite tradition on metal plates. A few men kept it, and then it was buried. It was never public monument writing, so we would not expect to find it.

Third, Brian Stubbs, a specialist in Uto-Aztecan, argues for about 1,500 proposed Semitic and Egyptian matches. He claims regular sound correspondences. That is the kind of evidence historical linguistics accepts.
no-semitic-inscriptions.rationaleLead: Strong for you: the small-record answer works, but it grants the claim cannot be tested.
no-semitic-inscriptions.rationale:
The small-corpus argument hangs together. It also grants that the claim cannot be tested.

Stubbs's work is the only positive evidence offered. No historical linguist outside the church has accepted it or engaged it seriously. The standard criticism is that his method searches a large word list for sound resemblances. Given enough candidates, that can turn up matches between unrelated families.

Meanwhile the null result stands. A whole field of decipherment has found no Afro-Asiatic link in any Mesoamerican script. Michael Coe of Yale has said so.

dna-native-american-origins.responseLead: A party of 30 joining a large population leaves no trace after 2,600 years.
dna-native-american-origins.response:
The church's own Gospel Topics essay grants that 'the majority of Native Americans carry largely Asian DNA'. It then answers on five fronts.

Nothing in the text says Lehi's party was the only population. The introduction was a 1981 editorial addition, not scripture, and 2006 corrected an over-reading.

A founding party of about 30 joining an already-large population would leave a signal below detection after 2,600 years. That is standard population genetics, not special pleading. Founder effect, drift and the bottleneck after contact each erase small founding lines. And we do not know the ancient Israelite genetic profile to look for.

Ugo Perego, a population geneticist, notes that the Asian ancestor of haplogroup X2a is itself undetected in modern Asia. Real founding lines do go missing. The essay's own bottom line is that DNA studies 'cannot be used decisively to either affirm or reject' the book.
dna-native-american-origins.rationaleLead: Take care: the science is sound, but their fix shrinks the Nephites to a tiny group.
dna-native-american-origins.rationale:
The population-genetics reply is technically sound. Drift, founder effects and the bottleneck genuinely can erase a small founding line. Critics who say DNA disproves the book overstate what a blank result can do.

The concession is still enormous. The defence works only by shrinking the Book of Mormon peoples into a marginal group inside a continent already full of Asians. That cuts against the text itself. 2 Nephi 1:8-9 has the land 'kept as yet from the knowledge of other nations'. It also cuts against 150 years of prophetic teaching.

And it took an unannounced edit to the printed introduction. That is the most concrete institutional concession in this whole list.

population-growth-impossible.responseLead: Smith answers Kunich well: a new colony with land to spare grows far faster.
population-growth-impossible.response:
James E. Smith is a trained historical demographer. He wrote in FARMS Review 6/1 in 1994. Kunich, he says, applies long-run averages to a young colony. That is the wrong yardstick. A frontier people with land to spare can hold 2 to 3% a year for centuries. Colonial New England did it. So did Pitcairn. Smith's own model runs reach Book of Mormon numbers on fair assumptions. Plural marriage among Lamanites and early Nephites would help too.

The strongest point is in the text itself. The book never says the land was empty. Sherem walks in from nowhere in Jacob 7. The Mulekites are found already numerous in Omni 1. And 'Lamanite' can work as a label for a side, not a bloodline. If Lehi's party joined peoples already there, no huge growth rate is needed.

Last, war dead in old records are famously inflated. That is true of the Bible, of Greece and Rome, and of the Maya. Reading those figures as a census is a mistake about what they are.
population-growth-impossible.rationaleLead: Weak on its own: Smith wins against Kunich, so use this only with DNA.
population-growth-impossible.rationale:
This is the criticism the Latter-day Saint side has answered best on its own terms. Smith is a credentialed demographer. His frontier-growth objection to Kunich is technically right, and the others-in-the-land reading is defensible from the text.

But the fix is costly, and it creates a squeeze. The more others you import to solve the demography and the DNA, the less the book is what its own narrators thought it was. Its nineteenth-century readers thought the same. And the text's total silence about a surrounding native majority becomes strange in itself.

On its own this does not sink the text. It works as a force multiplier on the DNA and archaeology entries.

translation-seer-stone.responseLead: The church now teaches the seer stone openly, in essays, Saints, and 2015 photographs.
translation-seer-stone.response:
Four replies, and the first is decisive. The church now teaches this openly. It is in the Gospel Topics essay, the Joseph Smith Papers, the Saints volumes, and the 2015 photographs in the Ensign. The sources were published in the nineteenth century and discussed in BYU Studies long before the internet found them. There was no suppression.

Second, 'Urim and Thummim' was used loosely at the time. It covered both the Nephite interpreters and the single stone. That makes the older telling imprecise rather than false.

Third, the method is beside the point in theology. If revelation is real, the instrument is incidental, and the Bible has comparable objects. Fourth, Skousen and Carmack argue the dictation was tightly controlled, which the seer-stone account supports.
translation-seer-stone.rationaleLead: This one is answered: the church teaches it openly now, so do not lead with it.
translation-seer-stone.rationale:
On the history, the church has conceded fully. The concession is in official curriculum now. Nobody disputes the facts.

Two things remain, and both are matters of meaning rather than evidence. The plates were not needed for the translation. That sits oddly beside the long story of digging them up and guarding them. And the stone that produced scripture is the stone he had used to hunt treasure.

The criticism as it is usually told, that the method was hidden, has been answered.

lost-116-pages.responseLead: Doing it again would never match word for word, and enemies held the only copy.
lost-116-pages.response:
Three replies. First, the stated reason is guarding against forgery, not dodging. If enemies held the only other copy, a fresh translation differing in any wording, as dictated translation always would, could be paraded as proof of fraud. Declining the trap is the rational move.

Second, the convenient-replacement framing ignores the text. The small plates are foreshadowed inside it, at 1 Nephi 9 and 19, as a second record made by Nephi. Mormon's plain 'I know not' why he included them reads like an old editor noting a prompting he did not understand. That is a strange thing for a forger to invent.

Third, believers read this as God providing ahead of a failure he foresaw. The episode is also the origin of a lasting lesson about Joseph's fallibility, in D&C 3.
lost-116-pages.rationaleLead: The forgery worry is fair, but no altered pages were ever published.
lost-116-pages.rationale:
This turns entirely on what you think likely to begin with. Both sides agree on every fact. Their reading hangs together, and the point about wording is genuinely right about how translation works.

The ordinary reading is still the simpler one, and it has one specific edge. The seer-stone method as the church now describes it has fixed English words appearing on the stone. That is a tight-control model, and under it a second try should have matched. So the wording objection loses its force.

Their defence and the church's own translation essay sit in mild tension. Nothing here can be settled either way.

witnesses-character-and-vision.responseLead: Not one of the eleven ever took it back, even when it would have cost nothing.
witnesses-character-and-vision.response: Four replies, and the first is the strongest fact on that side. Not one of the eleven ever took it back. That includes Cowdery, Harris and Whitmer, after bitter church trials threw them out. Taking it back then would have cost nothing and won them vindication. Whitmer never returned. Yet he restated it to hostile interviewers for 50 years, and had it carved on his gravestone. Second, the Eight Witnesses' account is plain and in daylight. They 'hefted' and 'handled' the plates. No angel was involved. That is a different kind of evidence, and the 'spiritual eyes' point does not touch it. Third, Richard Lloyd Anderson wrote Investigating the Book of Mormon Witnesses in 1981. He shows that 'spiritual eyes' in that century often meant real sight granted by the Spirit, as at 2 Kings 6:17. Most such quotes are late, secondhand, or hostile paraphrase. Fourth, the Whitmer point cuts the other way. A man who denounced Smith and never came back is the hardest witness of all to explain by social pressure.
witnesses-character-and-vision.rationaleLead: The best card they hold: treat it with respect, and do not call it settled.
witnesses-character-and-vision.rationale:
This one is genuinely two-sided. It is the strongest surviving Latter-day Saint position in this list. The record of never taking it back is real and not easily brushed off. Whitmer above all.

Against that, the witnesses were not outsiders. They were kin and business partners in one venture. Their view of knowing counted a vision as seeing. And Harris later gave the same kind of backing to the Shaker 'Sacred Roll'. That costs his word some of its value as a test.

Be wary of any source that calls this settled. The criticism is weaker than critics claim, and the answer stronger. But sincere men prove sincerity, not what was there.

gold-plates-never-examined.responseLead: Tumbaga is a copper-gold mix, and plates of that size would weigh what they said.
gold-plates-never-examined.response:
Apologists argue that the reported weight fits a real ancient object. Tumbaga is a copper-gold alloy, gilded at the surface, and it was used in Mesoamerica. Plates of the size described, made of tumbaga, would weigh roughly 53 to 58 pounds. They would look like gold. A forger guessing at 'gold plates' would be unlikely to land there.

The return to the angel is explained from scripture. The record was not meant to convince by proof. Ether 5 says witnesses were appointed instead. And Richard Lloyd Anderson's work shows those witnesses held to it for life.
gold-plates-never-examined.rationaleLead: Strong for you, but hand them the tumbaga point first, because it is a good one.
gold-plates-never-examined.rationale:
The core fact is conceded on all sides. No independent examination ever happened, and none is possible now.

The tumbaga answer makes the reported weight of 40 to 60 pounds add up, where solid gold that size would run well past 100. It still cannot stand in for the missing object.

What is left in dispute is only how much the insider witnesses can carry instead.

kinderhook-plates.responseLead: He made no translation at all, and the church itself published the hoax finding.
kinderhook-plates.response:
This is the church's own current published position. Joseph Smith never claimed a revealed translation, and never produced a translated text.

Don Bradley and Mark Ashurst-McGee, in 'President Joseph Has Translated a Portion' (2011), identify a specific character match against Smith's Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar. That makes the identification a plain comparison, not a revelation. Smith took the matter no further and dropped the subject. That is the opposite of a con artist walking into a baited trap.

The first-person wording is a known artifact of the History of the Church, which turned clerks' journals into Smith's voice. And the church published the forgery finding itself, in the Ensign in 1981.
kinderhook-plates.rationaleLead: This one is answered: use it about method, not as a knockout.
kinderhook-plates.rationale:
The Bradley and Ashurst-McGee work is decisive, and it is good scholarship rather than spin. The 'descendant of Ham' line traces to a character match against Smith's own Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar. So it was a plain comparison, not a revealed reading. And the church made the forgery finding public itself.

What is left is narrower than critics present. The match was still wrong, because the characters mean nothing at all. That bears on how far the Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar can be trusted.

And that leads straight to the Book of Abraham case, where the same papers are the problem. Treat Kinderhook as answered on its own terms.

source-parallels-voth-late-war.responseLead: Roberts drew no such conclusion, and 75 of the Late War matches are boilerplate.
source-parallels-voth-late-war.response: Three replies. Roberts drew no conclusion of dependence. He framed the work as questions a believer must be able to answer, and he died affirming the Book of Mormon. Using him for the prosecution misstates what he said. There is also no evidence Joseph Smith saw View of the Hebrews before 1830, and he cited it warmly in 1842 as support. That is how a man behaves who found it later. Second, the likenesses are generic to a whole genre of the 1820s about Hebrew origins for the Indians. The books differ on nearly every point. View of the Hebrews has no Christ, no story and no named people. And the Book of Mormon flatly denies the lost-ten-tribes idea it is built on. Third, on The Late War, 75 of the 'significant' matches come from the boilerplate copyright pages. The rest is mostly the King James register both books set out to imitate. The method detects 'wrote in biblical English'. The sharpest attack on it came from Ryan Thomas, who does not accept Book of Mormon historicity either.
source-parallels-voth-late-war.rationaleLead: Weak as stated: the ideas were in the air, but copying is not shown.
source-parallels-voth-late-war.rationale:
The direct-source claims are among the weakest material critics use. Hunting parallels across a huge body of books is unreliable. The copyright-page problem in the Johnson study is a real defect. And a critic himself rejects direct literary dependence. Roberts is routinely misused.

What survives is the modest version, and it is well supported. The Book of Mormon is at home in the religious culture of New England in the 1820s. Hebrew origins for the Indians. Anti-Masonic language. The fights over grace and universal salvation behind Alma 40-42.

That shows the ideas were in the air. It does not show copying. The King James and Isaiah dating entries are the strong textual case.

book-of-abraham-papyri.responseLead: Either the long roll is lost, or the papyri only prompted what God gave him.
book-of-abraham-papyri.response:
Two defences, both backed in the church's own essay.

The first is the missing-scroll theory, from John Gee and Kerry Muhlestein at BYU. The fragments we have are a small remnant. Eyewitnesses describe a long roll. Gee works out that about 314 centimetres of the Hor roll are missing. And much of the collection is thought to have burned in the Chicago fire of 1871. On that view the Abraham text sat on papyrus we do not have.

The second is the catalyst theory. Joseph's study of the papyri 'provided an occasion for meditation, reflection, and revelation'. God then gave him a revelation about Abraham 'even if that revelation did not directly correlate to the characters'.

Two supports follow. The Kirtland Egyptian Papers may be a later attempt by scribes to work backwards from a text already given. And apologists point to old parallels for content not in Genesis. Abraham nearly sacrificed. Abraham teaching the stars. And the name 'Olishem', which may match the attested place-name Ulisum. Those sit in traditions outside the Bible that Smith is unlikely to have known.
book-of-abraham-papyri.rationaleLead: Strong for you: the two defences are each fair, and they cancel each other.
book-of-abraham-papyri.rationale:
This is the strongest outside test in the whole corpus. The source document exists, and Egyptology is a mature science with no Latter-day Saint stake in it. The church has conceded the core fact in an official essay. Robert Ritner's complete edition of 2011 settled the reading.

The two defences each make sense alone. Together they are telling, because they contradict each other. Either the Abraham text was on a lost papyrus, which makes the translation real and the fragments beside the point. Or the papyri were only a prompt, which makes the lost scroll beside the point.

The missing-scroll theory has one problem it has not overcome. Smith's own Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar lines up characters from the surviving fragment against verses of the Book of Abraham. That puts his working source in documents we hold.

The catalyst theory cannot be tested. And it dissolves the word 'translation' as the church used it for 130 years, which drains force from the Book of Mormon claim too. Parallels such as Olishem are of the weak type flagged elsewhere, and cannot offset a direct mismatch in decipherment.

stylometry-wordprint-studies.responseLead: Schaalje showed the method must pick from your list; Rigdon and Spalding scored 0%.
stylometry-wordprint-studies.response:
G. Bruce Schaalje, a BYU statistician, and his colleagues found the decisive flaw. The method is a closed-set classifier. Its own maths obliges it to assign every chapter to one of the candidates you give it. Joseph Smith's own writings were largely left out of the pool, while Rigdon and Spalding were put in.

Schaalje extended the method so it could return 'author not in the set', and reran it on the same data. Rigdon and Spalding each scored 0%. The chance of an author outside the set came out at 93%.

Separately, the Spalding-Rigdon theory is rejected by nearly all historians of Mormonism, believers and non-believers alike. Fawn Brodie and Dan Vogel both reject it. The documents give Rigdon no traceable contact with Smith before late 1830, after the book was printed.
stylometry-wordprint-studies.rationaleLead: Neither side settles this: do not cite either study as proof.
stylometry-wordprint-studies.rationale:
This one is lopsided, and worth using as a lesson in method. The critical study is the weaker one. Schaalje's closed-set objection is correct, and mainstream historians reject Spalding-Rigdon on other grounds. Treat that study as answered.

But the studies on the other side do not therefore win. Telling several voices apart does not tell an ancient author from one writer making distinct characters. That is a known limit of the method on fiction. And the same 'author not in the set' logic cuts against any positive ancient attribution.

Stylometry as now practised cannot settle who wrote the Book of Mormon, in either direction. Discount confident claims from either camp.

jst-genesis-50-choice-seer.responseLead: The added verses need not be lost text; they can be given by God.
jst-genesis-50-choice-seer.response:
Latter-day Saint scholars grant that no ancient copy has the passage. Robert Matthews and Kent Jackson say so, and FAIR follows them.

Their argument is that the revision was never meant only to restore lost words. It can be restored content. It can be inspired comment. It can be a bringing together of texts, or a prophetic expansion shaped for a latter-day audience.

On that view, JST Genesis 50 may restore a real prophecy kept on the brass plates. That is why it also stands at 2 Nephi 3. It would have dropped out of the Hebrew line very early. Or it may be new content that was never in the Bible at all. Either way it rests on revelation, not on old copies.
jst-genesis-50-choice-seer.rationaleLead: Strong for you: the answer is honest, and it gives the point away.
jst-genesis-50-choice-seer.rationale:
The textual fact is conceded on all sides. No ancient witness contains the passage. Not the Hebrew, not the Septuagint, not a Dead Sea Scroll, not the Samaritan Pentateuch, not a targum. And the prophecy names the man who produced it.

The reply does not rebut the evidence. It reclassifies the revision so that missing manuscript support cannot count against it. That is untestable rather than a refutation.

angel-nephi-moroni-name-change.responseLead: It was a clerk's slip, and sources from 1835 already name the angel Moroni.
angel-nephi-moroni-name-change.response:
FAIR and church historians call the 'Nephi' reading a slip by a clerk or an editor. It came in when clerks put the history together in 1838 and 1839.

Sources before 1842 already name the messenger Moroni. Oliver Cowdery's 1835 letters in the Messenger and Advocate do. So does D&C 27:5, also from 1835. So Moroni comes first in the record.

Joseph Smith did not read the proofs of every instalment of the serialised history. And the church fixed the name to match the earlier, better-attested one. Nothing was covered up.
angel-nephi-moroni-name-change.rationaleLead: Arguable: a slip is likely, but that name stood in print from 1842 to 1853.
angel-nephi-moroni-name-change.rationale:
The print history is undisputed. It comes from the sources themselves. 'Nephi' stood in print from 1842 to 1853, and was later changed.

Their point that 1835 sources name Moroni first is also solid. That makes a clerk's slip quite likely.

What is left unexplained is why the slip ran on uncorrected through several official printings. It stood while Smith was alive, and after.

first-vision-multiple-accounts.responseLead: Retellings shift with audience and purpose, and the church now publishes all four accounts.
first-vision-multiple-accounts.response:
The church's Gospel Topics essay acknowledges all the accounts. It argues that the differences reflect audience, purpose and memory, rather than invention.

The 1832 account stresses personal forgiveness. The 1838 account stresses the founding of the church. Retellings that grow in detail are normal when a person tells his own story many times.

Historians such as Milton Backman and James Allen argue that the accounts fit together. 'The Lord' in 1832 can cover two persons. And several tellings with shifting emphasis point to a real core experience, rather than a story being built up.
first-vision-multiple-accounts.rationaleLead: Arguable both ways. The sharp point is that one person in 1832 became two.
first-vision-multiple-accounts.rationale:
The accounts and their differences are plain fact from the sources. The church itself now prints them.

What is argued is whether the differences are ordinary shifts of memory, or a story that grew. The sharpest of them are one person against two. And a search for forgiveness against a question about which church is true.

Trained historians argue both readings.

first-vision-revival-dating.responseLead: Backman found camp meetings near Palmyra in 1819 and 1820, across the wider region.
first-vision-revival-dating.response:
Milton Backman answered directly. He wrote 'Awakenings in the Burned-over District' in BYU Studies in 1969. He set out Methodist camp meetings near Palmyra in 1819 and 1820. He also found revival work across the wider Genesee region.

His point is that Smith described a stirring across a whole region. He did not describe a formal Palmyra revival with counted new members. The Gospel Topics essay takes that reading.

Smith was recalling his teenage years. He wrote of religious excitement in 'the whole district of country'. A Palmyra camp meeting in 1818, and an 1819 Methodist conference at nearby Vienna, fit that.
first-vision-revival-dating.rationaleLead: Arguable both ways. The Palmyra records came back blank, but the wider reading is fair.
first-vision-revival-dating.rationale:
Walters's blank finding stands largely unanswered in the church records. There was no 1820 Palmyra revival that added 'great multitudes' to the churches.

But Backman's camp meetings across the region in 1819 and 1820 give the 1838 account a fair looser reading.

It turns on how tightly you must read 'great multitudes' joining churches.

quitmormon-resignation-difficulty.responseLead: There is a free path in the Handbook, and real fake requests came first.
quitmormon-resignation-difficulty.response:
The General Handbook already sets out a free official path. A member writes to the bishop and asks that the record be removed. The request is to be honoured.

Leaders are told to check who the person is, and to make sure they know what follows. The church says those steps guard against fake or rushed removals. It says the 2019 notary rule came after real fake requests, including pranks that resigned other people.

Follow-up contact is care from lay leaders, who are taught to answer with love and not to pester. And any member may simply stop coming, with no penalty at all.
quitmormon-resignation-difficulty.rationaleLead: Strong for you, and keep it factual: what is argued here is motive, not fact.
quitmormon-resignation-difficulty.rationale:
The facts hold up. The scale of QuitMormon, on the order of 150,000 resignations since 2015, has been reported in the mainstream press. Both sides confirm the 2019 notary rule. And the reports of contact after leaving are many.

A legal buffer is the whole point of Mark Naugle's service, and it exists because of those reports.

What is argued here is motive: care for the member, or pressure to keep them.

temple-wedding-family-exclusion.responseLead: The temple asks the same of everyone, and the one-year wait went in 2019.
temple-wedding-family-exclusion.response:
The church holds that the temple is a sacred space, and that its ordinances ask for covenant worthiness. That is the same standard applied to everyone for any temple ordinance. It is not aimed at wedding guests.

The 2019 First Presidency change was made expressly so that 'when a temple marriage would cause parents or immediate family members to feel excluded, a civil marriage followed by a temple sealing is authorized'.

So couples may now hold a fully inclusive civil wedding first and be sealed straight after. The church presents that as solving the family problem while keeping the temple holy.
temple-wedding-family-exclusion.rationaleLead: They admit this: the 2019 letter names the very harm it was fixing.
temple-wedding-family-exclusion.rationale:
The rule and the old one-year wait are church policy, set down in writing.

The church's own 2019 letter names the harm it was easing. That change is a real improvement, and you should say so.

It also confirms the underlying claim rather than answering it. The recommend rule for a sealing has not changed. A parent without one still waits outside.

byu-honor-code-disaffiliation.responseLead: A private school may set its own terms, and tithing pays most of the cost.
byu-honor-code-disaffiliation.response:
BYU says it is a private religious school, paid for in large part by tithing. Latter-day Saint students pay a much lower fee, and the faith community makes up the rest.

The deal is stated up front. Stay in good standing with the church that funds you. Students agree to it when they enrol.

BYU notes that the accrediting bodies and the American Bar Association have upheld its right to set religious terms. An appeal route now exists for students who resign. And every student needs the yearly sign-off, including those who are not members. They just do not need to be members.
byu-honor-code-disaffiliation.rationaleLead: They admit this: the rule is in BYU's own papers, so argue about the name.
byu-honor-code-disaffiliation.rationale:
The policy is set out word for word in BYU's own papers. Leaving the church pulls the sign-off, and pulling the sign-off ends the right to stay enrolled. So the facts come from the school itself.

What is really in dispute is what to call it. A private school setting religious terms, or a penalty for changing your mind.

Ask it as a question, not as a charge.

social-costs-shunning.responseLead: There is no rule to shun, and Christofferson said he would not cut a child off.
social-costs-shunning.response:
Church leaders have spoken against cutting off family who leave, more than once and by name. Elder D. Todd Christofferson said in public that he 'would not cut that child out of family life'.

Official teaching tells members to keep loving and including family who go. There is no teaching, handbook rule, or discipline that tells a member to shun.

The church would add that broken ties follow a change of faith in many traditions. That is how families behave, rather than what the church asks.
social-costs-shunning.rationaleLead: Arguable, and both halves are true: real harm, but no order to shun.
social-costs-shunning.rationale:
The costs themselves are well attested, in reporting at NPR and HuffPost and in a great mass of first-hand accounts.

The harder claim is that the church causes them, and that one is genuinely argued. The written policy tells members not to shun. The teaching and the rhetoric can still push people apart. Boyd K. Packer's 1993 talk, naming 'so-called scholars', feminists and gays as dangers, shaped the mood.

Both things are true at once. The harm is real, and there is no order to shun.

grenfell-exit-testimony.responseLead: The church does not answer memoirs; visits are care, and the garment is a private covenant.
grenfell-exit-testimony.response:
The church does not answer memoirs by former members. Its standing position is that a member who steps away is still loved and still welcome.

Ministering visits are freely given care, and they stop when a person asks, or resigns. The garment is a sacred private covenant, taken freely in the temple. It is not a way of watching anyone.

Apologists would add two things. A paid ex-Mormon media career has its own pull. And one life should not stand in for a church of 17 million.
grenfell-exit-testimony.rationaleLead: Use with care: the pattern is documented, but one memoir is not proof.
grenfell-exit-testimony.rationale:
Her main claims hold up at the level of pattern. Contact after leaving, garment rules at General Handbook 38.5, and the social cost of going are all backed by church papers and by outside reporting.

The book itself is one person's word on particular events, and it is badged that way here.

It belongs on the site as a voice for a pattern that is documented. It does not stand as proof on its own.

ces-letter-gospel-topics-visibility.responseLead: The church did what critics asked, publishing frank essays on its hardest topics.
ces-letter-gospel-topics-visibility.response: The church did the thing critics had long demanded. It published frank, scholar-checked essays on its hardest topics, on its own website. It later folded that history into the official Saints volumes and the curriculum. No church had done that before. Elder Snow's account of the quiet rollout was pastoral, not secretive. Most members were not troubled by these issues. The essays were placed where a searching member would find them, without alarming those who were not asking. FAIR argues that the CES Letter is a shotgun list of recycled claims. Most of them, it says, are answered in the essays and in the apologetic literature.
ces-letter-gospel-topics-visibility.rationaleLead: Arguable both ways. The essays are real, but they still put Runnells on trial.
ces-letter-gospel-topics-visibility.rationale:
The timeline is settled. Elder Snow himself described the quiet rollout, and it is on the record.

Was that guarding people, or holding back? That is a judgement call, and the church did put the material out in the end. It counts for something.

Runnells was put on trial for a list of questions. That is on record too, and it sits badly beside the claim of openness.

september-six.responseLead: These councils are run by a stake president, and the charge was speaking out.
september-six.response:
FAIR and the church hold that discipline is run locally, by stake presidents. It is for conduct such as speaking out against the church and its leaders. That is apostasy as the handbook sets it out, and it is not scholarship as such.

They note that many working historians publish critical work and are never disciplined. The church does not run these councils from the centre.

The church also points to what came after, as a sign that it can take rigorous history. The Joseph Smith Papers. The Gospel Topics Essays. And Maxine Hanks being rebaptised in 2012.
september-six.rationaleLead: Strong for you: the dates, the six names and Packer's speech are not disputed.
september-six.rationale:
The six actions, their timing, and Packer's speech about three dangers are all on the record. No one disputes them.

What is argued is only how much was run from the centre.

As a claim about how the church met dissent, it stands.

sec-ensign-peak-settlement.responseLead: The church took legal advice, fixed the filings in 2019, and regrets the mistakes.
sec-ensign-peak-settlement.response:
The church's official statement says it took legal advice on how to meet the 13F rules while keeping the portfolio private. It cites scripture on keeping sacred gifts quiet and on avoiding show. It says it regrets the mistakes made.

When the SEC first raised a concern in 2019, Ensign Peak changed its filings at once. It now files a single form for the whole fund.

The church stresses what the settlement did not allege. No misuse of funds. No fraud against investors. No harm to members. It was a breach about forms, and the money is still set aside for the church's religious and charitable work.
sec-ensign-peak-settlement.rationaleLead: They admit this: the SEC order fixes the facts, so only the name is argued.
sec-ensign-peak-settlement.rationale:
The facts are fixed by the SEC order, and by the church's own settlement and public statement owning the mistakes.

The 13 shell companies, the $32 billion, and the wish to avoid bad press are all in the order itself. So is the finding that the First Presidency knew and approved.

All that is left to argue is what to call it. Poor legal advice, or a choice to hide.

nephite-non-levite-priesthood.responseLead: The Nephites held the Melchizedek priesthood, which the Bible puts before Levi.
nephite-non-levite-priesthood.response:
Apologists argue the Nephites held the higher Melchizedek priesthood. Jacob was ordained 'after the manner of his holy order' at 2 Nephi 6:2, and Alma 13 develops the idea. In the Bible that order comes before Levi and stands above it. See Genesis 14, Psalm 110, and Hebrews 7:4-10. So the rules about Levi did not bind them.

They add three things. The Book of Mormon never claims Levite authority for these priests. No Levites travelled with Lehi's party. And Jewish communities of exactly Lehi's era ran altars outside the Jerusalem system, at Elephantine and at Arad.

FAIR concludes the practice was not unthinkable for Israelites far from home.
nephite-non-levite-priesthood.rationaleLead: Small case: Alma 13 gives them a base, but Hebrews 7 keeps the tension alive.
nephite-non-levite-priesthood.rationale:
The Melchizedek reading has a base in the text itself, at Alma 13. And Elephantine gives real historical precedent for irregular practice far from home.

But Hebrews 7 treats a priesthood outside Levi as at odds with the law of Moses. And the Nephites claim to be keeping that law in all things.

So the tension between strict law-keeping and a non-Aaronic altar is not resolved.

temples-outside-jerusalem.responseLead: Jews did build temples far from Jerusalem. Elephantine and Arad were dug up.
temples-outside-jerusalem.response:
FAIR points to Jewish temples outside Jerusalem, from Lehi's own time or soon after. There was a temple with sacrifice at Elephantine in Egypt. There was a sanctuary at Arad. Leontopolis came later. So Jews far from Jerusalem did in fact build temples.

FAIR argues that the one-place rule of Deuteronomy 12 applied inside the land of Israel. It did not bind a group cut off from that land across an ocean.

On that reading Nephi's temple is what a devout but permanently separated colony would do.
temples-outside-jerusalem.rationaleLead: A minor one: the digs are real, but those altars were judged irregular.
temples-outside-jerusalem.rationale:
Elephantine and Arad are real sites, dug up and dated. They blunt the claim that this was unthinkable.

But scholars judge those altars irregular against the law of Deuteronomy. The Book of Mormon presents Nephite temples as fully proper.

So the clash with Deuteronomy 12 stands as a matter of law, even though the practice has precedent in history.

christ-remains-in-heaven-acts-3.responseLead: Christ appeared after the ascension to Stephen, Paul and John, so the verse permits it.
christ-remains-in-heaven-acts-3.response:
Apologists reply that the New Testament itself records Christ appearing after the ascension. He appeared to Stephen at Acts 7:55-56. He appeared to Paul on the Damascus road at Acts 9:3-6 and 1 Corinthians 15:8. He appeared to John on Patmos at Revelation 1:12-18.

So Acts 3:21 cannot mean Christ never appears before the restitution. It describes where he resides, not a ban on visits.

The Nephite ministry is claimed to be the same kind of appearance at larger scale. And 'other sheep I have' at John 10:16 is read as Jesus expecting it.
christ-remains-in-heaven-acts-3.rationaleLead: Do not use this one: their reply is simply correct, and it will cost you.
christ-remains-in-heaven-acts-3.rationale:
The strong reading of Acts 3:21, that Christ makes no earthly appearance until the end, is defeated by the New Testament itself. He appeared to Stephen, to Paul and to John.

Whatever other problems 3 Nephi has, and they are covered elsewhere, this verse does not rule out an appearance.

Christians should drop it.

joseph-smith-failed-prophecies.responseLead: Jonah said forty days and Nineveh stood. A word from God can carry a condition.
joseph-smith-failed-prophecies.response:
FAIR argues that prophecy in the Bible is often conditional without saying so. Jonah announced flatly that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown. It was not, and Jonah was no false prophet.

D&C 124:49-51, from 1841, puts that principle into their own canon. When enemies stop a commanded work, God 'requires that work no more'. The Saints were violently driven out of Jackson County in 1833, which made the temple impossible.

Other readings take 'an house' in verse 5 as fulfilled by the Kirtland temple in 1836. Or they treat the words as an order rather than a flat forecast.
joseph-smith-failed-prophecies.rationaleLead: Arguable both ways. It reads like a dated oracle, but D&C 124:49 sets a condition.
joseph-smith-failed-prophecies.rationale:
The non-fulfilment is not in dispute. And the formula 'this generation shall not all pass away' reads like a flat, dated oracle. Later leaders such as Orson Pratt kept restating it as one.

Yet the Jonah precedent is real, and the conditional clause at D&C 124:49 sits inside their own canon.

So this turns on how you read prophecy, not on a disputed fact.

word-of-wisdom-dietary-law.responseLead: It is a health code and a covenant standard, and any church may set one.
word-of-wisdom-dietary-law.response:
The strongest form of their position is this. The Word of Wisdom is not a purity law. It does not claim that certain substances defile the soul. It is a revealed health code and a covenant standard, resting on the body as a temple of God at 1 Corinthians 6:19-20.

Any covenant community may set such a standard as a condition of its own ordinances. The Bible has precedents. The Nazirite vow. Daniel's abstention. The Rechabites. All are commended.

The shift from counsel to commandment is explained as prophets applying it over time, by common consent, 'adapted to the capacity of the weak' at D&C 89:3. That is the same living authority they believe governed food rules in both Testaments.
word-of-wisdom-dietary-law.rationaleLead: Arguable both ways. The real question is advice that turns into a test of worthiness.
word-of-wisdom-dietary-law.rationale:
The history is not disputed, and church sources concede it. It was given 'not by commandment', and it later hardened into a gate for the temple, fixed under Heber J. Grant by 1921.

Whether that clashes with Scripture is argued. The health-code framing is coherent.

But Colossians 2:20-23 and 1 Timothy 4:3 take aim at exactly this: making abstinence rules a measure of standing. And here a rule about drink is tied to the ordinances held to be required for exaltation.

temple-garments-practice.responseLead: It reminds them of covenants, much as a habit, a collar or a prayer shawl would.
temple-garments-practice.response:
The church presents the garment as a private, personal reminder of covenants made in the temple. It offers the parallel of the nun's habit, the priest's cassock, the Jewish prayer shawl, and the Muslim skullcap. All are 'part of a rich tapestry of human devotion to God'.

The church notes that the tzitzit has the same stated purpose. Numbers 15:39 says the fringes are there 'that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD'.

Wearing it is framed as keeping a covenant freely made, not as a claim that clothing saves. And the statement in the recommend interview is read as being answerable for a covenant, not as legalism.
temple-garments-practice.rationaleLead: A minor case: the practice deserves respect, so ask about the checkpoint, not the cloth.
temple-garments-practice.rationale:
The practice, and the 2024 statement in the recommend interview, are documented from the church's own handbook at 38.5. Whether it clashes with Scripture is a question of judgement.

The tzitzit parallel is real in function. Both are a sign for remembering. But the tzitzit belongs to the Mosaic covenant, which Christians hold to be fulfilled.

And the Bible neither commands nor forbids such a practice for the church. So the criticism rests on inference, not on a direct clash. Treat the practice itself with respect.

exaltation-eternal-progression.responseLead: Early Christians taught theosis, and Jesus quoted 'Ye are gods' at John 10:34.
exaltation-eternal-progression.response:
The essay's strongest case is that this language runs through early Christianity. Psalm 82:6 says 'Ye are gods', and Jesus quotes it at John 10:34. 2 Peter 1:4 speaks of 'partakers of the divine nature'. Romans 8:17 speaks of being joint-heirs with Christ.

Church fathers from Irenaeus to Clement of Alexandria taught it. Clement wrote that the Word of God became man 'that thou mayest learn from man how man may become God'.

On that reading, exaltation restores an ancient doctrine of theosis rather than inventing many gods. Isaiah's denials are read as aimed at idols and rival gods, not at God's own children inheriting his nature. Exalted beings stay forever under the Father. And the essay stresses how little has been revealed about the first half of Lorenzo Snow's couplet.
exaltation-eternal-progression.rationaleLead: Strong for you, but handle theosis honestly: it always kept Creator and creature apart.
exaltation-eternal-progression.rationale: The teaching is established from their own canon and from the 2014 essay Becoming Like God. That essay rejects the planet cartoon while restating the substance: godhood, with the power to create. The theosis case does not close the gap. Deification in the fathers always kept the line between Creator and creature. It never taught that God was once a man. And it never made the deified gods in the sense D&C 132:19-20 describes. Isaiah 43:10 is left in direct tension. 'Before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.'

priesthood-temple-ban-1852-1978.responseLead: Nothing on record began it, a 1978 revelation ended it, and the old reasons are gone.
priesthood-temple-ban-1852-1978.response:
Their strongest case leans on the 2013 essay itself, and it is honest work.
