Joseph Smith ordained Black men. Elijah Able and Q. Walker Lewis are the named cases. The restriction arose under Brigham Young, amid the racial culture of 1850s America, with no recorded founding revelation. It was ended by genuine revelation to Spencer W. Kimball in 1978. And the church has since repudiated every reason it once gave.

Apologists draw a parallel from Acts. The gospel was withheld from Gentiles until Peter's vision. God lifts restrictions on his own timetable, through living prophets. And a church able to disavow its leaders' errors is showing revelation at work, not disproving it.
priesthood-temple-ban-1852-1978.rationaleLead: They admit this: the essay grants it all, and the question about prophets is left standing.
priesthood-temple-ban-1852-1978.rationale:
The history is fully documented, and the church's own essay concedes it. From 1852 to 1978 is 126 years. Six generations of real people carried it.

The Acts 10 parallel cuts against them. Peter's vision ended ethnic exclusion at the very start of the church. Here the ban came in after an open start. Prophets then defended it as doctrine for over a century. Its stated reasons are now disavowed.

That leaves the question about prophets standing.

endowment-masonic-origins.responseLead: Masonry was a catalyst. It gave him a ritual language for covenants God had given.
endowment-masonic-origins.response:
The church and FAIR grant the parallels, but separate form from substance. Masonry served as a catalyst. It gave Joseph a ritual language his hearers knew, in which to teach covenants that were truly revealed.

The content of the endowment has no match in Masonry. Creation. Fall. Redemption. And covenants of consecration. Unlike Masonry, it was given to women, and to 'even the weakest of the Saints'.

FAIR argues that the rite is the vehicle, not the endowment itself. So changing it, in 1990 and in 2019, is revelation going on rather than damage control.

And the temple is sacred, not secret. Its teachings are in print. Only certain signs and tokens are held back by covenant. Jesus too held some things back from the crowd, at Mark 4:34 and John 16:12.
endowment-masonic-origins.rationaleLead: They admit the dates: the catalyst reading reads those facts, it does not deny them.
endowment-masonic-origins.rationale:
The facts are documented, and the church's own essay effectively concedes them. Masonic initiation on 15 and 16 March 1842. The endowment seven weeks later, on 4 May. The shared elements. And the removal of the penalty oaths and the five points in April 1990.

The catalyst framing interprets those facts rather than rebutting them.

Note one thing more. The older defence, that the endowment was preserved from Solomon's temple, has quietly been dropped.

heavenly-mother-doctrine.responseLead: If we are truly God's children, a Mother follows, and the Bible's silence is not a denial.
heavenly-mother-doctrine.response:
The essay makes its case as a reasoned consequence of restored truth. David Paulsen and Martin Pulido back it in BYU Studies, with a survey of some 600 references through history.

The argument runs like this. Humans are literally God's spirit children. Genesis 1:26-27 makes them 'male and female' in the divine image. If parenthood there is eternal, a Mother follows.

Silence in the Bible is not denial. Latter-day Saints do not hold the Bible to be complete on doctrine.

And prayer still goes to the Father alone, in Christ's name, as Jesus taught. So she is honoured, not worshipped.
heavenly-mother-doctrine.rationaleLead: Strong for you, gently: the essay grants no Bible text and no recorded revelation.
heavenly-mother-doctrine.rationale:
The core fact is conceded in the essay itself. This is an affirmed doctrine resting on no biblical text and, by the church's own admission, on no recorded formal revelation.

The argument from consequence is coherent inside Latter-day Saint premises.

But it supplies no scripture. And scripture is the thing at issue.

jesus-firstborn-spirit-attained-godhood.responseLead: He is Jehovah, God before the world was made, and Paul calls him the firstborn.
jesus-firstborn-spirit-attained-godhood.response: Apologists reply that Jesus did not become divine late, or out of nothing that matters. He is Jehovah, the God of the Old Testament. The Living Christ of 2000 says so directly. He was fully divine before creation. He created 'worlds without number' under the Father's direction at Moses 1:33. And D&C 93:21 calls him 'the Firstborn' who was 'in the beginning with the Father'. On Colossians 1:15 they note that Paul himself calls Christ 'the firstborn of every creature'. FAIR argues that the Greek at Colossians 1:16 means organising material that already exists, not making from nothing. So 'all things were made by him' need not take in eternal spirit-matter, or Christ's own spirit. Firstborn status, they argue, means first place and heirship, as at Psalm 89:27. Latter-day Saint theology affirms that to the full.
jesus-firstborn-spirit-attained-godhood.rationaleLead: Strong for you, but give the Jehovah half first, then ask about John 1:3.
jesus-firstborn-spirit-attained-godhood.rationale:
The doctrine is documented from current official sources, and the clash is structural rather than a fight over one verse.

Grant that Christ as Jehovah was divine before the world was. This theology still makes him a begotten spirit brother of humanity whose divinity was attained. That is one of us who rose, rather than the eternal Creator who came down.

John 1:3 sweeps everything in. Colossians 1:17 says 'he is before all things'. Neither leaves a class of self-existing spirit-stuff, or sibling spirits, that Christ did not make. The Latter-day Saint reading has to carve out exactly what the text shuts off.

And the 'firstborn of every creature' point fails against verse 16's own reason: 'for by him were all things created'. He is first over creation because he made it.

jesus-lucifer-spirit-brothers.responseLead: A shared father means no parity. The Bible itself calls Satan a son of God.
jesus-lucifer-spirit-brothers.response:
FAIR concedes the taxonomy is 'technically accurate' but calls the framing misleading without context.

A shared spirit-parentage implies no parity. Cain and Abel were brothers, and nobody calls them equals. FAIR notes that the Bible itself calls Satan one of the 'sons of God', at Job 1:6 and 2:1.

Jesus is uniquely the first and greatest Son. He is the Creator of this world, and the Only Begotten in the flesh. Satan squandered what he had and became the eternal enemy of God.

The 2007 Newsroom statement takes the same line. Christ and Satan are 'diametrically opposite' in every attribute.
jesus-lucifer-spirit-brothers.rationaleLead: Strong for you, but drop the crude version: the point is what kind of being.
jesus-lucifer-spirit-brothers.rationale:
The teaching is documented from the canon at Moses 4 and Abraham 3, from the current manual, and from the church's own 2007 statement. That statement confirms the shared spirit-parentage rather than denying it.

Their reply rebuts the crude version, that Mormons think Jesus and the devil are alike. Nobody serious says that. It does not touch the real conflict, which is about what kind of being each one is.

In biblical Christology, Satan belongs to the class of made 'principalities and powers' that Christ himself made. Creator and fallen creature can no more be brothers of one species than a potter and his pot. And Job 1:6's 'sons of God' names angels in Yahweh's court, not begotten siblings of Yahweh.

So the moral-contrast defence answers a charge nobody serious is making.

god-exalted-man-flesh-and-bone.responseLead: 'God is a Spirit' speaks of mode, not anatomy, and the risen Christ has flesh.
god-exalted-man-flesh-and-bone.response:
FAIR argues that 'God is a Spirit' at John 4:24 states mode and character, not anatomy. It runs parallel to 'God is light' at 1 John 1:5 and 'a consuming fire' at Deuteronomy 4:24. Nobody takes those as the whole story.

Spirit and body are not opposites in any case. Risen beings have flesh and bone at Luke 24:39. FAIR marshals the appearances of God at Exodus 33:11 and 33:23. And David Paulsen of BYU argues that the earliest Christians thought of God in bodily terms, before Greek philosophy displaced that view.

On Adam-God, FAIR holds that Young's remarks were poorly recorded, speculative, or misunderstood. They were never canonised. And the church rejecting them shows living prophets correcting course, rather than prophecy failing.
god-exalted-man-flesh-and-bone.rationaleLead: Strong for you: take the verses as a set, and the Adam-God case cuts hard.
god-exalted-man-flesh-and-bone.rationale:
Every element is documented from canon or from current church publications. D&C 130:22 is canon. The 2014 essay confirms that the church still teaches the exalted-man doctrine.

The FAIR reading of John 4:24 has some force on its own. But the conflict rests on the verses taken together. A God who 'was once as we are now' cannot be God 'from everlasting to everlasting', or unchanging as Malachi 3:6 says. A God who rose inside an eternal frame of matter and law is not the Bible's Maker of all that is.

The Adam-God episode is on its own damaging to the self-correction reply. Young taught it plainly, again and again, over 25 years, including inside the temple. Kimball's 1976 denunciation means one prophet branded another prophet's pulpit teaching about God 'false doctrine'.

different-jesus-hinckley-1998.responseLead: He meant the Christ of the creeds, not the Jesus of the New Testament.
different-jesus-hinckley-1998.response: FAIR argues the quote is real but misused. In context Hinckley was marking off the Latter-day Saint Christ from the creedal Christ. That is the being of Nicaea and Chalcedon, without body and beyond grasp. He was not marking him off from the Jesus of the New Testament. Latter-day Saints insist they worship that Jesus as divine Son of God, Saviour and Redeemer. The Living Christ of 2000 says exactly that. The essay Are Mormons Christian? adds that the earliest Christian view of God 'changed dramatically over the course of centuries' under Greek thought. So holding to fourth-century creeds cannot be the test of who follows Jesus. They claim restored Christianity, not reformed Christianity. And on 2 Corinthians 11:4 they note that Paul's target was a different gospel message, not an exam on metaphysics.
different-jesus-hinckley-1998.rationaleLead: Arguable: the quote is real, but do not rest your case on one sentence.
different-jesus-hinckley-1998.rationale:
The quotation is real. It is in the church's own Church News of 20 June 1998, and Hinckley plainly affirms a real difference. That much is not in dispute, and the doctrinal entries back it up.

What this entry tests is the further step: that the sentence admits 'another Jesus' in Paul's sense. That is genuinely argued.

FAIR's point about context has real merit. 'Traditional Christ' most naturally means the creeds. And Latter-day Saint sources steadily identify their Christ with the Jesus of the New Testament: the same person, a different metaphysics.

Whether that counts as another Jesus should be argued from the doctrinal cases, not settled by this quote.

premortal-spirit-children.responseLead: Jeremiah 1:5, Job 38:7 and Hebrews 12:9 point to a life before birth.
premortal-spirit-children.response:
FAIR assembles a biblical case for life before birth. God knew Jeremiah 'before I formed thee in the belly', at Jeremiah 1:5. The 'sons of God shouted for joy' when the earth was founded, at Job 38:4-7.

At death 'the spirit shall return unto God who gave it', at Ecclesiastes 12:7. To return is to have been there. Hebrews 12:9 calls God 'the Father of spirits'. And the disciples' question about the man born blind, at John 9:2, seems to allow for choices made before birth.

FAIR adds that souls existing before bodies was a live view in early Christianity. Origen held it, and it was condemned only in the sixth century. On 1 Corinthians 15:46 they answer that Paul's subject is resurrection bodies, not where spirits come from.
premortal-spirit-children.rationaleLead: Strong for you, but grant them 1 Corinthians 15:46, which is about the risen body.
premortal-spirit-children.rationale:
The teaching is documented from current official sources, and the core conflict stands. No biblical text says human spirits were begotten by Heavenly Parents before the world. Zechariah 12:1 puts the forming of a man's spirit 'within him'.

The proof-texts thin out in context. Jeremiah 1:5 is the language of choosing and foreknowing, as at Romans 8:29. The 'sons of God' at Job 38:7 are angels, and God's point to Job is that Job was not there. 'Return' at Ecclesiastes 12:7 pairs with dust going back to earth.

FAIR is right about 1 Corinthians 15:46, so do not lean on it. And Origen shows the idea was thinkable early, though his version had no Heavenly Mother and no spirit birth.

The distinctive claim, that human spirits were literally born to heavenly parents, has no biblical support at all.

trinity-vs-godhead.responseLead: Jesus prays we may be one as they are one, which reads as relational.
trinity-vs-godhead.response: The strongest case runs on four fronts. First, Jesus prays that believers 'may be one, even as we are one', at John 17:20-23. Believers cannot merge into one substance. So the oneness of Father and Son in the same sentence reads most naturally as relational. That is the 'one in purpose' reading. Second, Jesus is visibly distinct from the Father all through the New Testament. At his baptism. In Gethsemane. In Stephen's vision at Acts 7:55-56. And 1 Corinthians 8:6 marks off 'one God, the Father' from 'one Lord, Jesus Christ'. Third, respected Christian philosophers model the Trinity as three centres of mind united in essence and will. Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne and William Lane Craig all do. BYU scholars argue that this lands close to Joseph Smith's Godhead. The quarrel, they say, is with Greek metaphysics added later, not with the Bible. Fourth, Hebrew work on the divine council in Psalm 82 shows plural elohim language native to the Old Testament.
trinity-vs-godhead.rationaleLead: Arguable: the John 17 reading is fair, but Isaiah 44:24 says he worked alone.
trinity-vs-godhead.rationale:
The doctrine is documented, and a real conflict exists. But their case has real merit at exactly the point this entry tests. The John 17 reading is defensible. Social trinitarianism is a live position among Christian thinkers.

The clash gets sharp where this doctrine goes further. Those thinkers still hold one uncreated divine essence. Here there are three separate beings. Two have bodies. At least one attained divinity. And exaltation hands godhood to others. Isaiah 44:24 and Isaiah 43:10 shut that out.

Note the strain inside their own canon. The Book of Mormon reads as strict monotheism at Alma 11:28-29, against Smith's later Nauvoo teaching.

It is graded contested because the John 17 argument works on its own ground.

blood-atonement.responseLead: That was Reformation preaching. It was never made canon, and the church dropped it in 2010.
blood-atonement.response:
FAIR and Mormonr answer on four fronts.

The blood-atonement language belongs to the heated preaching of the Mormon Reformation, in 1856 and 1857. It was overstatement, meant to stir people to repent.

It was framed as a free choice, and tied to a view of the death penalty for capital crimes, echoing Genesis 9:6. It was not tied to mob action. There is no evidence the church ever set up any system of killing sinners to save them.

It was never made canon. D&C 42:18 and 42:79 call for church trial and the civil courts, not ritual death.

And the church has since dropped it by name, in Bruce R. McConkie's 1978 letter and in the 2010 statement. It stands today as an abandoned guess from the 1800s.
blood-atonement.rationaleLead: Strong for you, gently: a prophet preached what the church now calls false.
blood-atonement.rationale:
Both the teaching and its disavowal are documented beyond dispute. The sermons are word for word in the Journal of Discourses at 4:53-54 and 4:219-220. And the 2010 statement shows the church understands what was taught well enough to disavow it by name.

What Young preached, that certain sins lie beyond the reach of Christ's blood, flatly contradicts Hebrews 10:14 and 1 John 1:7.

The hyperbole reading strains against his own words. They read as sober counsel across several sermons and several years.

The grade is medium because the doctrine is genuinely repudiated and carries no weight in salvation now. Its lasting force is as a second clear case, beside Adam-God, of a prophet teaching from the pulpit what the church now calls false doctrine.

js-polygamy-wives-count-ages.responseLead: The church grants the count, and Hales reads Helen's sealing as a family link only.
js-polygamy-wives-count-ages.response:
The church acknowledges the marriages. It frames them as a commanded restoration of Old Testament plural marriage, which Smith resisted. That is the setting of the accounts of an angel with a drawn sword.

Brian Hales argues that Helen Mar Kimball's sealing was likely 'eternity only' and dynastic, linking the Kimball and Smith families. There is no evidence of marital relations, and Helen went on living with her parents.

Marriage at 14 to 16, while young, was legal and not unheard of on the 1840s frontier.

And on the later accounts, Fanny Alger was a marriage with her parents' consent rather than an affair. Cowdery's words are those of an estranged critic.
js-polygamy-wives-count-ages.rationaleLead: They admit this: their answers go to what it meant, not whether it happened.
js-polygamy-wives-count-ages.rationale:
The core facts are conceded in the church's own essay. Between 30 and 40 wives. A bride of 14. And secrecy from Emma and from the church.

The replies go to what it meant, not to whether it happened. Eternity-only sealings. A dynastic purpose.

The eternity-only reading of the Kimball sealing is possible but cannot be proved. And frontier custom does not explain the concealment.

The claim as stated is documented by the institution itself.

js-polyandry.responseLead: Most were for eternity only, and DNA testing in 2016 cleared Smith of one claim.
js-polyandry.response:
Brian Hales argues that most of these sealings were 'eternity only'. They linked people for the next life without disturbing the earthly marriage. That is why husbands such as Henry Jacobs stayed in the home, and why some stayed faithful members.

There is supporting evidence. In 2016, DNA testing by Ugo Perego ruled Smith out as the father of Josephine Lyon. Her mother was the polyandrous wife with the strongest documentary claim of marital relations. No verified child of Smith by any plural wife has ever been identified.

And the essay itself states that these sealings may have been about eternal linking rather than earthly marriage.
js-polyandry.rationaleLead: They admit the sealings: do not claim proven sexual polyandry, you cannot support it.
js-polyandry.rationale:
The fact of sealings to married women is conceded by the church. Roughly 11 of them, about a third of his plural wives by Todd Compton's count.

Whether they included sexual relations is genuinely argued, and the DNA result is a real win for their side. Critics who assert proven sexual polyandry overreach.

But the claim as stated stands on primary sources. Sealings to other men's wives, under an angelic threat, and hidden from the community.

dc132-emma-destroyed.responseLead: 'Destroyed' is covenant language, and Emma refused and came to no harm.
dc132-emma-destroyed.response:
Apologists read 'destroyed' as covenant language rather than physical death. It means losing the blessings of the covenant, as verse 26 shows.

They note that no harm ever came to Emma. She refused, burned her copy of the revelation, and remained Smith's wife.

The revelation is framed as an Abrahamic test, and the verses addressing Emma also promise blessings for obedience. Richard Bushman notes that it was written down at Hyrum's request, specifically to persuade her.

On that reading it reflects a crisis in a household, not a death threat.
dc132-emma-destroyed.rationaleLead: They admit the text: the softer reading is fair, but the verse still stands.
dc132-emma-destroyed.rationale:
The text and its place in the canon are not disputed. Anyone can read it in the current Doctrine and Covenants.

The softened reading of 'destroyed' is a plausible gloss. It does not change what the section does.

Canonised scripture makes a named woman's fate turn on accepting her husband's other wives. Verse 52 commands it. Verse 54 warns her. Verse 64 extends that to any first wife who refuses.

js-polygamy-denials.responseLead: The denials were worded with care: he had one legal wife, and mobs were real.
js-polygamy-denials.response:
FAIR argues that the denials were worded with care. Smith denied adultery. He denied John C. Bennett's freelance 'spiritual wifery'. He did not deny the celestial marriage he believed God had given.

He had only one legal wife. So 'I can only find one' was true in a narrow sense.

Telling the truth openly would have brought mobs and charges. The Expositor affair proved it. So keeping it quiet shielded the community. Apologists point to Abraham, who misled a king about Sarah.

And the church's own essay grants the secrecy. It says those involved found it agonising.
js-polygamy-denials.rationaleLead: They admit the facts: a true sentence meant to mislead is still deception.
js-polygamy-denials.rationale:
The denials and the marriages that ran alongside them are both documented beyond dispute. On 26 May 1844 he said he could find only one wife. He had been sealed to more than 30 women.

Their defence concedes the deception and argues that it was justified.

A carefully worded statement made to create a false impression is still deception, by any ordinary or biblical measure. Proverbs 12:22 and Ephesians 4:25 are the texts. That is the claim being graded here.

eternal-polygamy-today.responseLead: Oaks says we do not know, and no one gets an eternity they do not want.
eternal-polygamy-today.response:
Dallin H. Oaks addressed this directly in General Conference in October 2019. The church makes no doctrinal claim about how families are arranged in the next life.

Trust in the Lord. Tangles in sealings will be resolved by a loving God, and nobody will receive an eternal arrangement they do not want.

Since 1998, deceased women may be sealed by proxy to all the men they married in life, on the assumption that the woman will choose. The restriction on living women is administrative, not a claim about eternal rank.

And the church has not practised plural marriage since 1904. It excommunicates those who do.
eternal-polygamy-today.rationaleLead: They admit the policy, and a candid 'we don't know' still settles nothing.
eternal-polygamy-today.rationale: The uneven rule, the leaders' own second sealings, and the canonical standing of D&C 132 are all public record and current Handbook policy. Russell M. Nelson was sealed to Wendy Watson in 2006. Dallin H. Oaks was sealed to Kristen McMain in 2000. Their reply is a candid 'we don't know'. That eases the pastoral weight, and it is worth respecting. It refutes nothing. The gap between what a widower may do and what a widow may do is still in force. Carol Lynn Pearson gathered the grief that follows in The Ghost of Eternal Polygamy, in 2016.

mountain-meadows-massacre.responseLead: Their own history says Brigham Young did not order it; his letter came two days late.
mountain-meadows-massacre.response:
The church fully acknowledges the massacre and its horror.

The setting was the Utah War. A federal army was on its way. The burnings in Missouri and at Nauvoo were fresh in mind, and wartime talk was everywhere.

The history the church paid for finds that Brigham Young did not order it. His letter, telling them to let the train pass, came two days late. Local leaders acted against that counsel. The cover-up was local first. Those who took part were later cut off from the church.

The church has built memorials. It has worked with the families of the dead. And it published the fullest account itself.
mountain-meadows-massacre.rationaleLead: They admit this: do not say Young ordered it, because the evidence does not go there.
mountain-meadows-massacre.rationale:
The massacre, its scale, and the planning by local church leaders are established by the church's own sponsored scholarship and by official statements. About 120 men, women and children were killed on 11 September 1857.

Critics who claim Brigham Young directly ordered it go beyond the documents. The church history concludes that he did not, though his war-hysteria preaching contributed.

The claim as stated is conceded by all serious parties. Church leaders at the Cedar City level planned mass murder.

nauvoo-expositor-carthage.responseLead: Oaks argues the city had legal footing, and Carthage was still an unjust killing.
nauvoo-expositor-carthage.response: Dallin H. Oaks published a legal analysis in the Utah Law Review in 1965. Before the Fourteenth Amendment, the First Amendment did not bind city governments. So abating the newspaper as a nuisance had some legal footing under the Nauvoo Charter. Oaks concedes that destroying the press itself likely went beyond that. The council feared the paper would bring a mob down on the city. The mob came anyway. On Carthage, defending yourself against a lynch mob with painted faces does not make an unjust killing just. Smith was in state custody under the governor's pledged protection. The pistol is recorded by the eyewitness John Taylor himself, and the church has published the fact, including in Saints. Martyrdom in the broad sense means being killed for your religion, not dying passively.
nauvoo-expositor-carthage.rationaleLead: They admit the facts: both are true, murder at Carthage and a paper telling the truth.
nauvoo-expositor-carthage.rationale:
Every element is documented in the Joseph Smith Papers, in History of the Church, and in the church's own topic essays. The accuracy of the Expositor's reporting. The mayor-ordered destruction on 10 June 1844. And the pepperbox at Carthage.

Apologetics contests the framing, martyr against man in a gunfight, and softens the legal question.

But the killing on 27 June was plainly murder outside the law. And the suppression of a truthful press was what set it off. Both things are true. Neither is refuted.

oath-of-vengeance.responseLead: The oath asked God to avenge, as the martyrs do at Revelation 6:10.
oath-of-vengeance.response:
FAIR emphasises that the oath asked God to avenge. It did not commit members to take vengeance themselves.

That runs closely parallel to the martyrs' cry at Revelation 6:10, 'How long, O Lord… dost thou not judge and avenge our blood?', and to the imprecatory Psalms.

It arose in the raw aftermath of the state-tolerated murders of Joseph and Hyrum Smith, for which nobody was ever convicted. It was removed as the wounds healed.

And temple ceremonies have always been revised. Its removal reflects the living, adaptive nature of the ordinances.
oath-of-vengeance.rationaleLead: Strong for you, but grant Revelation 6:10 first, then read Matthew 5:44.
oath-of-vengeance.rationale: Nobody informed denies that the oath existed. Its wording was given under oath in the Senate, at the Reed Smoot hearings of 1904 to 1906. David John Buerger set out the scholarship in Dialogue. It ran from about 1845 to about 1927, and was then quietly dropped. The Revelation 6:10 parallel is a fair answer to the caricature that this was an oath to do violence. Take that off the table first. What stands is the documented thing. A prayer for vengeance on a nation, taught to children to the third and fourth generation, inside the faith's holiest rite. Set that beside Matthew 5:44.

danites-1838.responseLead: Avard turned state's witness to save himself, which makes his word the least reliable.
danites-1838.response:
Avard was a self-aggrandising opportunist who turned state's witness to save himself. That makes his 'Smith was the mastermind' testimony as self-serving as testimony gets. He was excommunicated in 1839.

Leland Gentry and Alexander Baugh trace three phases. It began as legitimate community defence. Avard then corrupted it into secret oaths and plunder, without Smith's authorisation.

The 1838 setting was a fight for survival. Mormons were being burned out. Governor Boggs's Extermination Order and the Haun's Mill massacre followed within weeks. Mormon violence, while real, was a fraction of what was done to them.

And the church's own history topics acknowledge the Danite excesses.
danites-1838.rationaleLead: Arguable both ways. The raids are not disputed, but Smith's own orders are not shown.
danites-1838.rationale:
The Danites existed. Dissenters were driven out. Gallatin and Millport were raided and burned. None of that is disputed.

The load-bearing claim is that Smith told them to. That rests largely on Avard's tainted word, and serious historians divide. Stephen LeSueur on one side. Gentry and Baugh on the other.

Smith praised Danite leaders in public and rode the wave. Command of the operation is not shown. Contested is the honest grade.

policy-of-exclusion-2015.responseLead: Both were inspired answers to a moment. Neither was meant to stand for ever.
policy-of-exclusion-2015.response:
The church frames both the policy and its reversal as inspired answers to circumstances. Neither, on that view, is eternal doctrine.

The 2015 policy aimed to keep children out of the crossfire between home and church. The same reasoning already applied to the children of polygamists.

By 2019, leaders concluded through continued revelation that it caused more harm than it prevented. Continuing revelation allows a change of course by its very nature. Apologists cite Acts 10 as the pattern, where the shutting out of Gentiles is reversed.

Policies carry out doctrine for a time and a place. The doctrine of marriage beneath them never changed.
policy-of-exclusion-2015.rationaleLead: They admit it all, including the words 'will of the Lord' in 2016.
policy-of-exclusion-2015.rationale:
Every fact is on the record. That includes Nelson's own 'mind of the Lord and the will of the Lord' framing in January 2016. It shuts off the easier defence, that the 2015 change was only policy.

The argument that continuing revelation can reverse course is coherent on its own terms. But it concedes the sequence rather than refuting it.

Four years, and families carried the cost between. What that implies about revelation is for the reader. The record itself is not in dispute.

tithing-enforcement.responseLead: There is no paid clergy here, and Malachi 3:8-10 calls withholding it robbing God.
tithing-enforcement.response:
The church has no paid local clergy. Bishops, teachers and leaders all serve free. So tithing funds operations, chapels, temples, education, and a large welfare and humanitarian programme.

Members widely testify that tithing is a blessing rather than a burden.

Tithing also long predates this church. Malachi 3:8-10 frames not paying it as robbing God, so gating on it has a biblical case.

The Huntsman ruling vindicated the church's statements. The court found no misrepresentation. City Creek was funded from earnings on invested reserves, exactly as President Hinckley had said. And the declaration is self-reported. Nobody audits your income.
tithing-enforcement.rationaleLead: They admit the structure, and the fraud claim was thrown out 11 to 0.
tithing-enforcement.rationale:
The recommend question, the yearly declaration, D&C 64:23, and the gating of exaltation ordinances are all in current church publications. None of it is contested.

The critics' strongest overreach was the fraud theory. James Huntsman's suit was dismissed 11-0 by the full Ninth Circuit in January 2025. Do not repeat it.

The core claim is simply a description of current practice. Ordinances held to be needed for salvation are conditioned on a payment. Set that beside 2 Corinthians 9:7.

missionary-program-realities.responseLead: Service is freely chosen, and the flat $500 keeps Tokyo and Peru the same.
missionary-program-realities.response:
Service is freely chosen, and it is framed as consecrated service rather than work.

The flat payment levels it out. A missionary in Tokyo pays what one in Peru pays, and ward funds cover those who cannot.

Huge numbers of returned missionaries call it the making of them. A language learned. A habit of discipline. A life turned toward service.

The rules exist for safety and focus, as they do in monastic and military life. And the 2019 changes, with weekly calls and looser schedules, show the church listening to how missionaries fare.
missionary-program-realities.rationaleLead: They admit it all, and it is low stakes: mention it, do not press it.
missionary-program-realities.rationale:
Every element comes from the church's own publications. The $500 a month since 2020. The rules. And the two calls a year before February 2019.

Their case is real too. It is freely chosen, and the benefits people report are genuine. Calling it unpaid labour understates how much people want to go.

But the claim describes facts the church itself confirms. The severity is low because the practice is open, and consented to.

prophetic-fallibility-unfalsifiable.responseLead: They teach that prophets are men. Not every sermon is a word from God.
prophetic-fallibility-unfalsifiable.response: The church expressly teaches that prophets are fallible men. Joseph Smith said that 'a prophet is only a prophet when acting as such'. Not every sermon is revelation. Young's musing about the moon and sun was flagged as opinion. He said 'I rather think it is'. And it matched mainstream science of his century, since William Herschel believed the sun inhabited. It was never canonised or made a test of faith. Mormon Doctrine was a private book McConkie published without approval. Its correction and its withdrawal show the system correcting itself rather than failing. And Woodruff's statement, in context, answered a specific fear that the Manifesto was apostasy. It promises that God would remove a president who tried to lead the church fundamentally astray. It does not promise that presidents never err.
prophetic-fallibility-unfalsifiable.rationaleLead: Pick Adam-God. The moon quote and Mormon Doctrine are weak, and you will be corrected.
prophetic-fallibility-unfalsifiable.rationale: The quotations are real and can be checked. But the force of the claim depends on whether these were held out as prophetic, and their case has real substance. Young flagged the moon and sun remark as opinion. Mormon Doctrine was never official, though it needed over 1,000 corrections and still sold for decades before being pulled in 2010. Adam-God is the strong example. It was taught in conference as doctrine and later disavowed, and it keeps the tension live. The unfalsifiability point against Woodruff's line is fair philosophy. As a claim of failed prophecy, this is genuinely contested ground.

abuse-helpline-2022.responseLead: By Arizona law that confession was private. The state's high court agreed in 2023.
abuse-helpline-2022.response:
The church calls the AP framing egregiously wrong.

The bishop repeatedly urged Adams and his wife to report, and tried to intervene. Arizona law made the confession privileged. He legally could not pass on what he learned in it without consent. Arizona's courts agreed. In 2023 the state supreme court upheld the privilege and dismissed the claims against the church.

The help line exists so that untrained lay bishops reach professionals at once. Those professionals instruct them to comply with reporting laws, which vary by state. The church says its first priority is protecting victims.

And others knew. The mother knew, and so did people who saw what Adams posted online. They did not report either.
abuse-helpline-2022.rationaleLead: Arguable, and handle with care: the timeline is fixed, the cause is not.
abuse-helpline-2022.rationale:
The core timeline is established by court records and is not disputed. A confession in 2011. No report. Seven more years of abuse, coming to include a second daughter, an infant, until Adams was caught independently in 2017.

The claim about cause is genuinely argued. Did the help line exist to shield the institution ahead of children? The legal advice tracked Arizona's actual privilege statute, the courts sided with the church, and the bishops' bind was real.

What remains is that the system's design produced a catastrophic outcome, and that these calls route through defence counsel. Whether that is malice, negligence or compliance is the contested question.

kirtland-safety-society.responseLead: Hundreds of banks fell in the Panic of 1837, and Smith lost his own money.
kirtland-safety-society.response:
FAIR and church historians argue five things.

The 1830s were the age of unregulated wildcat banking. Hundreds of banks, many of them chartered, failed in the national Panic of 1837. So the collapse reflects the economy rather than fraud.

The charter was refused for Ohio party reasons. Hard-money Democrats turned down nearly every new charter that session, and anti-Mormon feeling may have added to it. Operating as a joint-stock anti-banking company followed legal advice under law that was genuinely unsettled.

Joseph Smith put in more of his own money than almost anyone, and lost heavily. That is not the profile of a swindler. He resigned in June 1837 and warned the Saints against the notes before the worst of it.

And Woodruff's journal does not record what the revelation said. The grand line about swallowing up all banks comes only from Warren Parrish, by then a hostile ex-member with his own alleged part in the failure.
kirtland-safety-society.rationaleLead: They admit the facts: 'all would be well' was falsified within months.
kirtland-safety-society.rationale:
The load-bearing facts are conceded in the church's own publications. The Joseph Smith Papers and the Church History Topics essay grant it all. The refused charter. The choice to operate anyway. The October 1837 fines for illegal banking. Smith's flight. And that leaders bore blame.

The revelation claim rests on a faithful source, not a hostile one. Wilford Woodruff wrote it in his own journal on 6 January 1837. Smith attached the word of the Lord, and an audible voice, to a venture that failed within months. It was ruled illegal. And 200 to 300 members left.

Their case genuinely softens the question of intent. Fraud is not shown. The Panic of 1837 was real, and Parrish deserves discounting.

It does not touch the core problem under Deuteronomy 18:21-22. A promise that all would be well was falsified by events.

post-manifesto-polygamy.responseLead: The Manifesto spoke of United States law. It said nothing about other nations.
post-manifesto-polygamy.response:
The church's own Gospel Topics essay makes the case, and concedes most of the record.

After October 1890, plural marriages 'continued to be quietly performed' in Mexico and Canada. The Manifesto stated President Woodruff's intention to obey the laws of the United States. It 'said nothing about the laws of other nations'.

Leaders in good faith read it as a legal document. They did not read it as a ban on the principle everywhere. 'Many Church leaders believed the Manifesto merely suspended plural marriage for an indefinite time.'

Husbands already married kept living with their plural wives, and fathered children well into the next century. They did not cast off covenant families. Only in 1904, with the Second Manifesto, were members put on notice. Taylor and Cowley were then dropped from the quorum.

Apologists add three points. Turning away from what leaders believed God had commanded was wrenching. It happened while the federal government hunted them. And muddle, not plotting, explains the fifteen-year lag.
post-manifesto-polygamy.rationaleLead: They admit nearly all of it, and a church president admitted it under oath.
post-manifesto-polygamy.rationale:
This is the rare case where the church's own essay concedes nearly every element. Marriages quietly performed with leader involvement. Cohabitation and children. The Manifesto's limited legal scope. Two apostles removed.

And Joseph F. Smith's sworn Smoot testimony of March 1904 is a first-person admission by a church president. Five plural wives, and eleven children by them since 1890.

What their case reframes is sincere confusion against duplicity. It cannot erase that leaders publicly and repeatedly denied what they privately authorised. The Second Manifesto's 'sanction, consent or knowledge' claim is falsified by Quinn's roughly 250 and Hardy's 262.

Nor can it erase that this replays the Nauvoo pattern. Measured by Proverbs 12:22 and Ephesians 4:25, the pattern stands conceded in substance and argued only in motive.

facsimile-1-lion-couch.responseLead: The hole covers the very figures in dispute, so nobody knows what stood there.
facsimile-1-lion-couch.response:
John Gee, Kerry Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central argue four things.

First, the hole means nobody knows what the original showed. Some hold that the papyrus was already torn in 1835. A knife and a human head could have stood there. They add that this scene is odd for its type. The figure on the couch looks alive and clothed, with both hands perhaps raised.

Second, Egyptian temple texts do show enemies ritually killed. So a sacrifice reading is not absurd.

Third, Jews living in Egypt plainly reused Egyptian pictures and gave them new meanings. So this scene could have gone with an Abraham text, whatever it was first drawn for.

Fourth, on the catalyst view the papyri were only a prompt. That makes the explanations inspired comment, not Egyptology.
facsimile-1-lion-couch.rationaleLead: Arguable, unlike the other two. The hole sits right where the argument is.
facsimile-1-lion-couch.rationale:
Unlike Facsimiles 2 and 3, this one has a real gap in the evidence. The hole covers exactly the disputed parts. So the restoration case runs on parallels and ink traces, not on a surviving original.

The scholarly reading is far better supported. Anubis, in a routine embalming scene from Hor's Breathing Permit. Ink traces of a headdress at the shoulder. Hundreds of parallel scenes. And no parallel at all with a knife in it. The church's own essay grants that Egyptologists read it differently.

But they dispute what filled the hole, not the Egyptology. And the scene does have odd features. So this figure is scored contested.

Note the labels around it, though. The jars as gods of foreign nations, and the crocodile as Pharaoh's god, have no support at all.

facsimile-2-hypocephalus.responseLead: Min was a god who made life, and these amulets do carry cosmic meaning.
facsimile-2-hypocephalus.response:
Latter-day Saint scholarship concedes that figure 7 depicts a form of Min. Rhodes, Gee, Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central all grant it. They then argue three things.

First, Min was for Egyptians a supreme creator god. He stood for the power that makes life. So 'God sitting upon his throne' may catch the figure's role in Egyptian religion, even if the image shocks a modern reader.

Second, hypocephali are esoteric objects. They encode cosmic geography and rebirth. A cosmological reading is therefore not alien to the genre. A few of Smith's labels are argued to land near Egyptian ideas, such as figure 1 as the creative force at the centre, and figure 4 as the firmament.

Third, under the Semitic-adaptation and catalyst frameworks, the explanations were never meant as decipherment. They were inspired reuse, in the way Egyptian Jews reused pagan imagery.
facsimile-2-hypocephalus.rationaleLead: Strong for you: their own scholars grant figure 7 is Min, and no rival reading exists.
facsimile-2-hypocephalus.rationale:
There is no dispute about what figure 7 is. Their own sources name it as Min, shown with an erect phallus.

The dispute is only whether Smith's label can be rescued. Can 'God sitting upon his throne, revealing the grand Key-words of the Priesthood' be read as a fair gloss on a fertility god approached by a serpent? No Egyptologist reads one of these amulets as teaching Kolob, key-words, or the Holy Ghost.

Michael Rhodes is a Latter-day Saint scholar. His own reading of the rim and panels gives ordinary funeral prayers for Sheshonq.

Their case does not meet the translation evidence. It moves the explanations outside translation, which gives the point away. Smith said he translated by the gift and power of God. The checkable claims fail checking.

facsimile-3-presentation.responseLead: They accept the readings, and say Jews reused the scene for their own story.
facsimile-3-presentation.response:
The strongest case comes from Gee, Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central. It offers no rival reading of the captions. It accepts them, and argues that the figures were relabelled.

First, in Egyptian thought Pharaoh stood for Osiris on earth. Isis could be tied to the throne itself, and even to the king. So Isis as Pharaoh has some precedent.

Second, Jews in Egypt plainly took Egyptian scenes and used them for their own figures. Abraham turns up in later Egyptian magic texts. So an old Jewish editor could have relabelled this as Abraham at court.

Third, scenes of this kind do dress one figure in another's imagery. So crossing gender in a label is not unknown.

Fourth, some of the glyphs are copied badly in the woodcut. The Isis name group is one. That clouds what stood on the original.
facsimile-3-presentation.rationaleLead: Strong for you: he said the name is written above the head, and it says Isis.
facsimile-3-presentation.rationale:
This is the hardest facsimile case for their side. Smith staked his labels on the characters themselves: 'whose name is given in the characters above his head'. Those characters can now be read. They say Isis and Maat. Not a Pharaoh. Not a prince. Where Smith saw 'Shulem the waiter', they name Hor, who owned the papyrus.

No source on their side offers a rival reading. Théodule Devéria reached the same result in 1860. So did the 1912 panel that included Flinders Petrie and James Breasted.

Their answer accepts the Egyptology and posits an old relabelling that no document shows. Not on this papyrus.

The church's own essay grants that Egyptologists read it differently from Smith. It stops short of granting error. So the verdict is unrefuted rather than admitted.

adam-god-doctrine.responseLead: The sermons survive in rough transcripts, and it was never made canon.
adam-god-doctrine.response:
FAIR argues that Young's sermons survive only in rough transcripts. It argues that he taught other things that do not fit a strong Adam-God reading. And it notes that the teaching was never made canon by common consent.

On that account it was one man's private speculation. It was not church doctrine.

Kimball's 1976 denunciation is presented as the system working. The living church corrects itself. Doctrine is set by scripture and by the united voice of the First Presidency. It is not set by every pulpit remark of a past president.
adam-god-doctrine.rationaleLead: They admit this: one prophet called another prophet's temple teaching false doctrine.
adam-god-doctrine.rationale:
Kimball's 1976 denunciation concedes the substance. Something Young taught as doctrine is now officially 'false doctrine'.

The misreporting defence fails against several independent records. The Journal of Discourses. Young's own reaffirmation in 1873. Wilford Woodruff's journal. And the St George temple lecture minutes of 7 February 1877.

The remaining move, that it was never canonised, rescues the church's doctrinal process only by conceding the evangelistic point. A president of the church, speaking as prophet, taught for 25 years, including inside the temple, something the church now denounces.

That collapses 'the prophet will never lead the church astray' as a working guarantee.

priesthood-restoration-late-account.responseLead: The 1832 history speaks of angels, and they had good reason to stay quiet.
priesthood-restoration-late-account.response:
FAIR and BYU scholars reply on four fronts.

Joseph's 1832 history does mention receiving 'the holy Priesthood by the ministring of Aangels'. And an 1829-era revelation, now D&C 27, points to authority from heavenly messengers.

Joseph and Oliver kept the details quiet because they were being hunted. Joseph said they were 'forced to keep secret the circumstances of having received the Priesthood'.

The 1835 additions are framed as a prophet making his own earlier words clearer, under the same inspiration.

And Whitmer and McLellin were hostile by then. They were recalling events forty or fifty years on.
priesthood-restoration-late-account.rationaleLead: Arguable both ways. The 1835 growth is plain, but hidden events are still possible.
priesthood-restoration-late-account.rationale:
The documented facts favour the critics. The named-angel account appears nowhere before Oliver Cowdery's in October 1834, five years later. And the 1835 additions are visible in the church's own Joseph Smith Papers.

But their case is not empty. The 1832 history's 'ministring of Aangels' phrase is a genuine, if unclear, counter. So is the persecution-secrecy argument. And late hostile memories do deserve discounting.

What is beyond dispute is the retroactive growth of the text. What stays arguable is whether it records suppressed events or invents them.

That split is the definition of contested, though the pattern matches the First Vision's shifting accounts.

book-of-commandments-revisions.responseLead: He never claimed the words were dictated, so he could reword them later.
book-of-commandments-revisions.response:
FAIR argues that Joseph Smith never claimed the words were dictated by God. Revelations came as impressions, put into his own imperfect language.

So the man who received them could revise them, expand them, and update them as the church grew. The additions to section 20 simply took in offices revealed after 1830.

The church prints every version openly in the Joseph Smith Papers. FAIR calls that the opposite of a cover-up.

And the revised texts were accepted by common consent at the 1835 conference.
book-of-commandments-revisions.rationaleLead: They admit this, but a text that can be re-engineered later carries less weight.
book-of-commandments-revisions.rationale:
The changes are conceded and published by the church itself. The Joseph Smith Papers put both editions side by side, and FAIR's defence justifies the edits rather than denying them.

The remaining dispute is what to make of it. May a prophet revise God's words? And there their answer creates its own problem.

If revelations are Joseph's fallible paraphrases, open to later re-engineering, then the weight of any given 'thus saith the Lord' drops. That includes D&C 132.

Severity is medium because the fact bites chiefly alongside the priesthood-restoration backdating.

egyptian-alphabet-grammar.responseLead: The scribes worked backwards from an English text already given, and never published it.
egyptian-alphabet-grammar.response:
Gee, Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central argue that the borrowing runs the other way.

On their view the scribes were working backwards. They had an English text already given, and tried to build Egyptian out of it. It was a study exercise Joseph allowed but did not write.

Most pages are in scribes' hands. The Grammar was never printed and never made canon. And they argue that the Abraham text came first, on the evidence of the manuscripts.

So the Kirtland Egyptian Papers show 1835 curiosity about Egyptian. They do not show how the Book of Abraham was made.
egyptian-alphabet-grammar.rationaleLead: Arguable on which came first, but his own journal says he arranged that grammar.
egyptian-alphabet-grammar.rationale:
The narrow question is which came first: the English text, or the Alphabet documents. That is genuinely debated. Joseph Smith Papers editors call the documents intertwined, and scholars on both sides make textual arguments.

So the strongest critical framing, that the Grammar was the engine of translation, stays contested.

But the escape is expensive. Joseph's own journal says the group was 'arranging a grammar of the Egyptian language'. Either way, his circle produced an Egyptian system under his eye, and it is nonsense.

Set beside the papyri mismatch, this backs up the case rather than carrying it alone.

zelph-white-lamanite.responseLead: Joseph wrote nothing, the diaries disagree, and the printed version is a later blend.
zelph-white-lamanite.response:
FAIR, drawing on Kenneth Godfrey's source study, notes that Joseph himself wrote nothing about Zelph.

The six diary accounts disagree on key details. Which battle it was. Whether the Rocky Mountains phrase was original.

The History of the Church version is a later scribal blend that hardened a casual campfire comment into formal revelation.

And even taken at face value, apologists argue that Zelph could be a late-period Lamanite in the hinterlands, far from the Book of Mormon's core lands. So the story does not fix Book of Mormon geography.
zelph-white-lamanite.rationaleLead: Arguable on details, but all six diaries agree on the core claim.
zelph-white-lamanite.rationale:
The objections about sources are real. The accounts do differ on details, and the printed version is a blend. So the exact wording of Joseph's statement cannot be recovered. That keeps this out of unrefuted.

But all six diaries agree on the core. Joseph claimed a vision naming a specific skeleton as a white Lamanite under a prophet called Onandagus.

That core is either a false claim of revelation about a Hopewell burial, or it must be watered down to guesswork. That is the same untestable move seen elsewhere.

Contested on the details. Damaging on the pattern.

bom-geography-retreat.responseLead: The text never names a modern place, and the distances in it require a small map.
bom-geography-retreat.response:
Apologists respond that the text itself never names a modern location. They add that the travel distances inside it actually require a limited geography.

So the hemispheric model was a cultural assumption early members laid over the text. Joseph among them, speaking as a man. It was not revelation.

Scripture Central argues that a Mesoamerican setting meets dozens of textual tests. Writing systems. Cities. Warfare. Population.

And the church's official neutrality is fitting humility on a question scripture leaves open. They compare it to unresolved questions in biblical geography.
bom-geography-retreat.rationaleLead: Strong for you. Believers now pull apart each other's maps, using the same arguments.
bom-geography-retreat.rationale:
The retreat is documented in the church's own 2019 statement. It 'does not take a position on the specific geographic locations'.

The defence that the text never names a place fails against canon. The Doctrine and Covenants is scripture, not speculation, and D&C 28:8, 32:2 and 54:8 name North American tribes as Lamanites. Prophets taught the New York Cumorah as doctrine.

The strongest sign that no answer works is the apologists themselves. FAIR and Scripture Central publish refutations of the Heartland model. Their arguments mirror the critics' case against Mesoamerica. The Heartland side returns the favour.

When every proposed place is convincingly refuted by fellow believers, the claim has become untestable by moving it.

polygamy-coercion-angel-sword.responseLead: Hales says the story shows he held back. Women did refuse, and paid no price.
polygamy-coercion-angel-sword.response:
Brian Hales and FAIR argue that the angel accounts come from faithful participants, and that they show Joseph's reluctance. He delayed for years and acted only under divine compulsion. That is the opposite of a predator's eagerness.

They note that Helen Mar Kimball's sealing was likely unconsummated and dynastic. It linked families for the next life only.

They note that women such as Sarah Pratt and Cordelia Morley refused Joseph with no spiritual penalty. That shows real agency.

And they argue that marriage customs for young women in the mid-1800s were sharply different from ours. Modern categories of coercion do not map cleanly onto them.
polygamy-coercion-angel-sword.rationaleLead: They admit the facts: the answer itself is that an angel threatened him into it.
polygamy-coercion-angel-sword.rationale:
The essential facts are conceded in the church's own essay. The drawn-sword angel. Helen's marriage 'several months before her 15th birthday'. The sealings to already-married women. The salvation promise to Helen comes from her own faithful memoir.

The threats in D&C 132:54 and 64 are canon.

Their reframing disputes what it meant, not what happened. And 'an angel threatened him into it' is itself the admission. The proposals carried a promise from God and a threat from God at once.

Galatians 1:8 speaks to exactly the case of an angel authorising another gospel. 2 Corinthians 11:14 warns that Satan appears as an angel of light. The severity is high because this goes to character, and to the fruit test of Matthew 7:15-20.

holocaust-proxy-baptisms.responseLead: The dead may accept or refuse, and each violation broke stated church policy.
holocaust-proxy-baptisms.response:
The church and Mormonr reply that proxy baptism forces nobody. The teaching is that the dead may take it or refuse it. So it is an offer, not a conversion after death.

The church kept the 1995 agreement. Each case on record was one member acting against a stated rule.

And the church acted. It took names out. In 2010 it built blocks into the database for Holocaust victims. It said sorry to families. And it warned that anyone doing it again may lose temple access, or face a church court.
holocaust-proxy-baptisms.rationaleLead: They admit this, and handle it gently: these are real families.
holocaust-proxy-baptisms.rationale:
Every load-bearing fact is conceded by the church itself. The practice happened. The 1995 agreement existed. Violations went on for two decades. And the church publicly condemned and apologised for specific cases, including Anne Frank and the Wiesenthals.

The individual-members defence is fair as far as it goes. It also concedes the systemic point. A doctrine that makes ordinances for the dead 'essential to our salvation' creates a pressure that policy could not hold for twenty years.

The deeper use here is doctrinal. The whole temple-for-the-dead system hangs on one disputed verse, 1 Corinthians 15:29. Read it against Hebrews 9:27, Luke 16:26, and even Alma 34:32-35.

prop-8-campaign.responseLead: Churches may speak on moral questions, and members gave freely as private citizens.
prop-8-campaign.response:
The church's Newsroom and FAIR respond that churches have always had the right, and a duty, to speak on moral questions. Marriage is a moral question, not partisan politics.

The church endorsed no candidate and no party. It joined a broad interfaith coalition rather than acting alone. Catholics, evangelicals, Orthodox Jews and Muslims were in it.

Direct institutional spending was a small, disclosed, in-kind amount. Members donated freely, as private citizens.

And D&C 134 also says governments should protect the free exercise of conscience. That, the church argues, is what it was doing.
prop-8-campaign.rationaleLead: They admit the facts: press D&C 134:9, not the general charge.
prop-8-campaign.rationale:
The facts are documented and not denied. The First Presidency letter of 29 June 2008. The fundraising through church channels. The roughly $20 million from members, about half the Yes campaign's funds. And the FPPC fine for late reporting.

The defence justifies the involvement rather than disputing it, so the substance is admitted.

Whether religious political advocacy is wrong is a judgement Christians themselves divide over. So the force here is narrower. It lies in the mismatch with D&C 134:9. And it lies in the pattern of mobilise, then soften. Proposition 8, the 2015 exclusion policy, the 2019 reversal, then the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act.

huntsman-tithing-lawsuit.responseLead: Hinckley's own talk named earnings on reserves, so no juror could find fraud.
huntsman-tithing-lawsuit.response:
The church's defence, accepted by the full court, is that Hinckley's 2003 statement drew a line. It distinguished tithing itself from 'earnings of invested reserve funds' and from commercial-entity money.

City Creek was funded from the latter. So there was no misrepresentation, let alone fraud. Huntsman produced no evidence that tithing principal was spent.

The concurring judges added a second ground. The First Amendment's church-autonomy doctrine forbids civil courts from judging what a church tells members about sacred donations at all.
huntsman-tithing-lawsuit.rationaleLead: Do not use this one: it lost 11 to 0, and on the merits.
huntsman-tithing-lawsuit.rationale:
After full argument on both sides, the fraud theory failed 11-0 on 31 January 2025. For a majority it failed on the merits, not on constitutional avoidance.

Hinckley's own wording at the time anticipated the distinction between earnings and principal.

So what is left is whether earnings on invested tithing are morally still tithing. That is a quarrel about words, not a proven deception. Honest grading calls this answered. The church won this one.

The broader transparency concern is real, but it belongs to the SEC and Ensign Peak case, which stands on its own.

paul-h-dunn-fabrications.responseLead: That was one man's failure, not policy. He was censured and made to apologise.
paul-h-dunn-fabrications.response:
FAIR replies that Dunn's lying was his own failure, not church policy.

The church looked into it. He was censured. He was moved to emeritus status. And he was made to say sorry in public. That is being held to account, not a cover-up.

Latter-day Saints do not claim their leaders never sin. One man's dressed-up sermons say nothing about whether the Restoration is true. A pastor who lies does not disprove Protestantism either.

His apology, and the church taking it, model what repentance looks like.
paul-h-dunn-fabrications.rationaleLead: They admit this, and it proves little: use it small, about how testimony works.
paul-h-dunn-fabrications.rationale:
Dunn's own printed confession of October 1991 settles the facts. So does the censure he owned up to. The church's own Deseret News reported both.

FAIR is right that one leader's sins do not falsify a faith. That is why the severity is low.

The value here is as a pattern, not as proof. It shows how a faith-promoting story works. A strong tale stirs a strong feeling, and the hearer takes that feeling as proof. And it shows a taste for quiet handling, 'for reasons of age and health', until a reporter forced it out.

Use it to open the question of how we know things.

hofmann-forgeries-church-response.responseLead: Seeing is not knowing everything. The best document men in the country were fooled.
hofmann-forgeries-church-response.response:
FAIR replies that discernment is not the same as knowing everything. God does not shield leaders from ordinary human deceit, and Scripture shows prophets fooled in plain matters.

The best document men in the country were fooled too. So were dealers and historians.

The church bought papers as any archive buys papers about its own past. It printed several of them, the salamander letter among them, rather than burying them. And it worked with the prosecutors.

Leaders being willing to handle troubling papers is framed as openness. Hofmann's success says something about forgery. It says nothing about revelation.
hofmann-forgeries-church-response.rationaleLead: They admit the sequence: D&C 46 promises discernment so the church is not deceived.
hofmann-forgeries-church-response.rationale:
The sequence is conceded in the church's own essay. The meetings. The purchases. The vault. The failure to detect. And the murders of Steve Christensen and Kathy Sheets in October 1985.

Only the meaning is disputed. The reply that discernment is not omniscience has force against a cheap gotcha. But it prunes the claims of the office. D&C 46:23-27 promises the discerning of spirits precisely 'lest ye be deceived'.

And look at what leaders did. They negotiated for and secured documents that undercut their own founding story. They found a magic-salamander origin plausible enough to buy.

That they treated the salamander letter as possibly genuine Martin Harris material says something about the folk-magic world it came from.

burning-in-bosom-epistemology.responseLead: Asking God is biblical. James 1:5 says ask, and the two on the road felt it.
burning-in-bosom-epistemology.response:
FAIR argues that personal revelation is thoroughly biblical. 'Ask of God', says James 1:5. Hearts burned on the Emmaus road, in Luke 24:32. Peter's testimony came 'not by flesh and blood', in Matthew 16:17.

The witness is not raw emotion. It is knowledge borne by the Spirit. And D&C 9:8 commands study first, so the feeling confirms the work rather than replacing it.

Other faiths having spiritual experiences is to be expected, since God gives light to all people. Such experiences may soften a heart toward God in general, without tying a person to one specific claim.

And critics who reduce every spiritual experience to brain chemistry prove too much. That would undo Christian conversion too.
burning-in-bosom-epistemology.rationaleLead: Strong for you: their own answer grants a feeling may not tie you to one claim.
burning-in-bosom-epistemology.rationale:
Their reply defends the claim that God can speak, and the Christian gladly grants it. It never answers the actual objection. How does a feeling tell true claims from false ones, when religions that contradict each other produce the same feeling?

FAIR makes one concession that costs a great deal. It grants that spiritual experiences may not tie a person to one specific claim. That is exactly the use Moroni 10:4 is put to. The missionary programme treats the feeling as certifying a whole set of very specific claims.

And Deuteronomy 13:1-3 shuts the move off in principle. Even a real supernatural sign must yield to testing by doctrine.

This is arguably the keystone case. Every other entry here can be waved off by appeal to the testimony this method produces.

chiasmus-alma-36.responseLead: Two physicists ran the numbers. Alma 36's order is very unlikely by chance.
chiasmus-alma-36.response: Boyd and Farrell Edwards are physicists. They published a study of the odds. They estimate it is very unlikely that Alma 36's repeated elements would fall into that mirror order by chance. Their method, they argue, does not rest on Welch's or Wunderli's literary judgements. Apologists add that the shape fits the meaning. Conversion sits at the centre of a life told backwards. They argue that the candidates in the Doctrine and Covenants are plainly weaker. And they note that nothing puts John Jebb's Sacred Literature of 1820, or any work on chiasmus, in Joseph Smith's hands in rural New York before 1829.
chiasmus-alma-36.rationaleLead: Concede the pattern and contest what follows: a shape does not make a book old.
chiasmus-alma-36.rationale:
This is a real two-sided exchange in peer-reviewed journals. Wunderli's point about picking and choosing lands. But the Edwardses' reply on the odds is a serious counter, and it survives his rebuttal in part.

Calling it contested, rather than dismissing it, is both true and good for your credibility.

The deeper point is this. Even grant a deliberate chiasm in Alma 36. The step to antiquity still fails. A writer soaked in King James parallels could produce a mirror shape, and modern texts have them.

A shape on the page cannot outweigh the anachronisms, the DNA and the textual evidence. Concede the pattern. Contest what follows.

nahom-nhm-altars.responseLead: The altars date the NHM tribe to Lehi's era, right where the text turns east.
nahom-nhm-altars.response:
Warren Aston and Scripture Central argue that NHM is rare as an Arabian place name. The altars independently tie the tribal name to precisely Lehi's period and region. That was unknowable from 1820s New York.

They note that no evidence connects Joseph Smith to Carsten Niebuhr's maps.

And they stress the chain of hits. A burial place bearing a Semitic root that carries the sense of mourning and consolation. Positioned exactly where the text turns the party east. Ending at plausible candidates for Bountiful on the Omani coast.

That chain, they argue, multiplies well beyond coincidence.
nahom-nhm-altars.rationaleLead: Their best single piece of evidence. Give it full weight, then ask about America.
nahom-nhm-altars.rationale: Honesty requires ranking this as their best single datum. It is a real inscriptional match, correctly dated and plausibly located. It is also weaker than it is usually presented. A tribal name of three consonants. A root common in Semitic naming. A turn that follows the trade route everyone took. And a form of the name, Nehhm, on published European maps in English by 1792. Archaeology outside Mormonism sees nothing evidentiary in it. Philip Jenkins wrote that 'there's no there there'. Both sides field serious arguments from real data, which is the definition of contested. Grant Nahom its full weight. Then note that one consonant cluster in Arabia cannot offset the total absence of Nephite evidence in the New World, where the story's thousand years unfold.

succession-crisis.responseLead: The keys went to the Twelve, and most of Nauvoo sustained them in August 1844.
succession-crisis.response:
Apologists answer that succession did not depend on family. Joseph conferred the keys of the kingdom on the Quorum of the Twelve before his death. On 8 August 1844 the great majority of Nauvoo Saints sustained the Twelve over Rigdon.

Strang's letter of appointment is judged a forgery on handwriting and postal grounds. Apologists contend that several Voree witnesses later distanced themselves from Strang.

On Emma, FAIR argues that her denials are contradicted by heavy documentary evidence, including sealing records naming her participation in 1843. They explain them four ways. She wanted to protect her sons. She opposed polygamy. She was in property disputes with Brigham Young. And she was loyal to the movement her son led.

Family closeness, they note, is not the biblical test of truth.
succession-crisis.rationaleLead: Strong for you, but note the cost: their answer needs Emma lying for 35 years.
succession-crisis.rationale:
Every fact here is conceded on all sides. No written plan for succession was produced. Emma and the Smith family rejected Brigham Young. Joseph Smith III led the rival RLDS church from 1860. And Emma denied polygamy to the end, in her 1879 'Last Testimony'.

The keys-to-the-Twelve argument has real historical support. Most of Nauvoo did follow the Twelve.

But the defence costs more than its makers say. It requires holding that the prophet's own widow lied in public, steadily, for thirty-five years. Meanwhile friendly witnesses are treated as beyond question.

And the usual way of dismissing Strang's plates, and witnesses who never took it back, fits the Book of Mormon's own witnesses just as well.

second-anointing.responseLead: Sacred, not secret: the blessing is conditional, and the same hope is held out to all.
second-anointing.response:
Defenders do not deny that the ordinance exists. They defend its privacy.

Mormonr frames it as sacred rather than secret. It is treated with the same reserve as other temple matters. It is not a plot.

They note that the Bible anoints individuals. Priests and kings were anointed. And Jesus spoke of mysteries given to some and not to others.

They stress that the blessing is conditional. It is not a flat guarantee, so it does not remove the need to endure in faith.

The rarity, they argue, is prudence about a blessing that could be misread. And ordinary members lose nothing. The same blessings are held out to all the faithful, and what is missed in this life may be received later.
second-anointing.rationaleLead: They admit it all: the only argument is over the word secret.
second-anointing.rationale:
This is graded admitted because their own side confirms every factual element. The ordinance exists. It is given by invitation of the highest leadership. It is absent from public teaching. And members are explicitly instructed not to discuss it.

The only dispute is what to call it, sacred against secret, and whether a conditional sealing differs much from a guaranteed one.

The force here is untouched by that framing. A two-tier system, in which an inner circle receives a hidden assurance ordinary members do not know exists, stands in stark contrast to the New Testament.

There, assurance is proclaimed openly and offered to all believers on the basis of faith in Christ. 2 Peter 1:10 addresses every reader of a public letter, not the initiates of a private rite.

jst-whole-bible.responseLead: It was a first pass, never finished, and hundreds of readings are in the footnotes.
jst-whole-bible.response:
FAIR and BYU scholars respond that the July 1833 statement marked the end of a first pass. It was not a finished book. Joseph kept revising until his death in 1844, and never prepared a manuscript for the press.

The order to publish, at D&C 124:89, went unmet amid poverty and persecution. So the church inherited a working draft, not a finished Bible.

They add that the revision was never meant as one uniform restoring of lost words. It blends restoring, prophetic comment, harmonising and modernising. That explains the gaps against Book of Mormon readings.

And far from hiding it, the church put hundreds of its readings in the footnotes and appendix of its 1979 edition. The 2024 purchase shows reverence, not shame.
jst-whole-bible.rationaleLead: Arguable, but his own record says he finished it in 1833.
jst-whole-bible.rationale:
The core facts are undisputed. The revision was commanded. It was pronounced finished in Joseph's own record in 1833. It was commanded to be published in 1841. It was never canonised. And it was published instead by the rival denomination that rejected Brigham Young.

Their reply, that it was actually unfinished and mixed in genre, is a genuine scholarly position. Joseph did keep tinkering. That keeps this contested rather than unrefuted.

But the defence sits awkwardly with the sources. It must read 'we this day finished the translating of the Scriptures' as not meaning finished. And it concedes that the revelation commanding publication was never obeyed.

The category problem stays on any reading. A prophet corrected the Bible by revelation, and the church claiming his mantle still hands members the uncorrected King James.

lectures-on-faith-decanonized.responseLead: They were lessons, not revelations, and were pulled so members would not confuse them.
lectures-on-faith-decanonized.response:
FAIR, and Joseph Fielding Smith, who sat on the 1921 committee, argue that the Lectures were lessons rather than revelations.

They were never claimed as the word of the Lord. They were incomplete on the Godhead. And they were removed to keep members from confusing them with actual revelations.

On this view, 1921 was housecleaning rather than de-canonisation.
lectures-on-faith-decanonized.rationaleLead: They admit this: one question does the work, and there is no revelation behind it.
lectures-on-faith-decanonized.rationale:
The response concedes the key facts. The 1835 assembly voted to accept the entire book, lectures included, as 'the doctrine and covenants of their faith'. The claim that they were never accepted as more than lessons is contradicted by the 1835 record itself.

And 'incomplete on the Godhead' is a euphemism. Lecture 5's spirit-Father theology was superseded, and the canon was trimmed to match.

This pairs powerfully with D&C 132, which stays in the canon while being disavowed. The canon is edited by administrative decision, not by revelation.

It comes down to one question. What revelation removed them? There is none.

independence-temple-lot-ownership.responseLead: The temple will still be built, and D&C 124:49 covers a work enemies prevented.
independence-temple-lot-ownership.response:
The church teaches that the Independence temple will still be built, in the Lord's timing.

D&C 124:49 provides that when enemies prevent a commanded work, God no longer requires it of that generation.

The church's own question-and-answer page affirms continued belief in a future temple in Zion. It also notes cordial relations with the Temple Lot church.
independence-temple-lot-ownership.rationaleLead: They admit the ownership: nothing stops them building, except who owns the spot.
independence-temple-lot-ownership.rationale:
The D&C 124:49 escape clause cannot explain the present tense. Nothing prevents the church from building in Jackson County today. Nothing, that is, except that it does not own the prophesied spot, and the owners will not sell. They have refused offers for over a century.

A 194-year-old 'center place' prophecy whose ground is held by a tiny rival body of about 7,000 members is vivid, checkable in five minutes, and hard to spin.

It is graded on the ownership core, which every party grants, including the church's own materials. Do not argue the dating here. That belongs with the failed-prophecies case.

zions-camp-dc105-reversal.responseLead: D&C 103 was always conditional, and the march shaped the men who later led.
zions-camp-dc105-reversal.response:
Apologists read D&C 103 as conditional.

D&C 105 itself explains why. The Saints failed to consecrate, and they were not ready. So the Lord deferred the promise rather than broke it.

Zion's Camp is then reframed as a refining trial. Many future apostles and seventies were chosen from among its veterans. On that reading the march succeeded at its real purpose.
zions-camp-dc105-reversal.rationaleLead: Strong for you, and unusually clean: both halves sit in their own scriptures.
zions-camp-dc105-reversal.rationale:
The conditions were announced after the failure, not before it. D&C 103 reads as a flat promise with divine backing behind it. 'Mine angels shall go up before you.' D&C 105 fits the conditions on once the march collapsed.

The refining-trial reading concedes that the stated goal failed.

The unique value here is teaching value. Unlike disputed prophecy cases, the believer's own canon holds both the promise and the walk-back. No outside source is needed. And a 'little season' now entering its third century speaks for itself.

one-mighty-and-strong.responseLead: The 1905 statement settles it: the verse was about Edward Partridge and land in 1832.
one-mighty-and-strong.response:
The 1905 First Presidency statement holds that the verse was about one situation in 1832.

It concerned Bishop Edward Partridge, and who would inherit land in Zion. It was likely mooted when Partridge repented.

And anyone who claims the title today 'manifests great ignorance' of God and of the order of the church.

Church materials treat the matter as settled by that statement.
