one-mighty-and-strong.rationaleLead: A small one: do not lead with it, but the 1905 press release is telling.
one-mighty-and-strong.rationale: The 1905 statement is itself the interesting fact. For 73 years the verse sat open, and it bred claimants. A Dialogue survey documents about eighteen main ones, and at least eight had declared themselves by 1905. Then the First Presidency closed a canonised prophecy by reinterpreting it in a newspaper. That is a move of authority, not a reading members could have reached from the text. This is not a lead argument. Use it as backing, on how the canon handles a prophecy that did not come true. It is directly useful when fundamentalist offshoots come up, since nearly every splinter prophet has drafted this verse.

lorenzo-snow-couplet-status.responseLead: He answered narrowly. Little has been given on it, so the church says little.
lorenzo-snow-couplet-status.response: Apologists say Hinckley was answering narrowly. The church does not stress or elaborate the doctrine, because little has been revealed about it. He was not denying it. Hinckley told the next General Conference that the news reports were 'incomplete'. And the 2014 essay Becoming Like God affirms that humans can become like God, while noting that scripture says little about God's past.
lorenzo-snow-couplet-status.rationaleLead: Strong for you, and it is about candour: a manual teaches what the prophet downplayed.
lorenzo-snow-couplet-status.rationale: Grade this on the candour gap, not on the doctrine itself. The doctrine is the exalted-man case, covered separately. The same church that publishes a prophet's manual built around the couplet had its sitting prophet tell national media 'I don't know that we teach it'. Either the prophet did not know his own doctrine, or he was managing its public image. Both are problems for a church claiming prophetic clarity. Ronald Huggins, in the Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society in 2006, traced the couplet's use in church curricula. So 'we don't really teach it' is documentedly false. This is conversationally strong. Most members have learned the couplet, and showing them Hinckley's answer tends to land.

evolution-shifting-statements.responseLead: The 1909 letter was about our divine origin. It was not about the science.
evolution-shifting-statements.response:
The church holds that the 1909 statement was about where humans come from. It affirmed a divine origin. It did not pick a mechanism in biology.

The 1910 and 1925 materials show openness.

The church takes no official position on evolution itself. It leaves science to science.

BYU's evolution packet, approved by its board, reflects that neutral stance.
evolution-shifting-statements.rationaleLead: Arguable. Never say they banned it, but their apostles split for seventy years.
evolution-shifting-statements.rationale:
Do not claim that the church banned evolution. It never quite did, and the neutrality framing has real support, in the 1910 Christmas message and in the BYU packet.

The strong core is narrower and solid. Apostles taught flatly opposite positions on a factual question for seventy years, while all claiming prophetic authority. Joseph Fielding Smith and Bruce R. McConkie on one side. James E. Talmage and B. H. Roberts on the other.

And the no-death-before-the-Fall scripture stands uncorrected while being quietly abandoned. See 2 Nephi 2:22, Alma 12:23-24, Moses 3:7 and D&C 77:6-7.

Use it as a case study in how prophets settle empirical questions. They did not. The scientists did, and the church followed. Corroboration, not your lead.

mormon-name-reversal.responseLead: The Lord named the church in D&C 115:4, and prophets get updated direction.
mormon-name-reversal.response:
Nelson taught that the Lord named the church in D&C 115:4, and that restoring the full name honours Christ. See also 3 Nephi 27:7-8.

The earlier nickname campaigns were well-intentioned accommodations to public awareness.

And prophets can receive updated direction, line upon line, without their predecessors being condemned. Nelson said the change was 'not a name change… it is a correction' commanded by the Lord.
mormon-name-reversal.rationaleLead: They admit the facts, so keep it light: a small, recent, always-live example.
mormon-name-reversal.rationale:
This is a soft case doctrinally, but it is documented end to end from church sources. And it is constantly live in conversation. Why can't we say Mormon anymore?

Its value is as an accessible, low-stakes specimen of the pattern the bigger cases show. A prophet framed a reversal of his predecessors' publicly taught position as timeless divine will. And he attached the word Satan to what the church itself did until that year.

Use it as a gentle door-opener, not a centrepiece.

avoid-worship-joseph-smith.responseLead: They worship the Father and the Son; the hymn honours a founder, and is not worship.
avoid-worship-joseph-smith.response:
That is false as stated. Latter-day Saints worship God the Father and Jesus Christ. They do not worship Smith.

The church explicitly denies worshipping him, and members experience the accusation as an obvious misrepresentation of their own lives.

'Praise to the Man' is veneration of a founder. Its language is admittedly extravagant, 'mingling with Gods'. But it is not liturgical worship.
avoid-worship-joseph-smith.rationaleLead: Do not use this one: you would be wrong in your very first sentence.
avoid-worship-joseph-smith.rationale: Opening with 'you worship Joseph Smith' is factually wrong, corrected in ten seconds, and it marks you as someone who has never sat with a Latter-day Saint. Here is what is true and useful instead. Everything distinctive in Mormonism rests on Smith's claims. Joseph Fielding Smith wrote that 'Mormonism, as it is called, must stand or fall on the story of Joseph Smith'. That is Doctrines of Salvation 1:188. Say that. The test is whether Joseph told the truth, and the church agrees that is the test. It is a door the member's own leaders opened.

avoid-coca-cola-ownership.responseLead: Snopes debunked it, and Ensign Peak's filings list no Coca-Cola at all.
avoid-coca-cola-ownership.response:
It is an urban legend, and flatly false.

Snopes traces it to the appeal of a delicious irony. No ownership stake has ever existed. Ensign Peak's post-settlement 13F disclosures list no Coca-Cola, no PepsiCo and no Keurig Dr Pepper holdings.

The legend also rests on a second error. The church never banned caffeine.
avoid-coca-cola-ownership.rationaleLead: Do not use this: a debunked legend hands your friend a free win.
avoid-coca-cola-ownership.rationale:
Repeating a legend that Snopes has debunked hands the member a free win. It also taints everything else you say.

The documented finance story is far stronger. Ensign Peak's concealed reserve of more than $100 billion, and the 2023 SEC settlement, are already on this site as admitted and adjudicated fact.

If church money is the topic, go there. 'The SEC fined your church for hiding $32 billion behind shell companies' needs no urban legend's help.

avoid-magic-underwear-mockery.responseLead: The church calls that phrase inaccurate and offensive, and answered it in 2014.
avoid-magic-underwear-mockery.response: The garments are real and the practice is documented. That case is on this site. But 'magic underwear' is mockery, not argument. The church's 2014 video Sacred Temple Clothing pre-empts exactly this line. It compares garments to the nun's habit, the prayer shawl and the monk's robe, and calls the phrase 'inaccurate and offensive'. Folk beliefs about physical protection do exist among members. They are not official doctrine.
avoid-magic-underwear-mockery.rationaleLead: Never use this one: it makes you the aggressor and ends the conversation.
avoid-magic-underwear-mockery.rationale:
Mocking someone's underclothing makes the Christian the aggressor. It triggers the persecution frame the church has already built a video around. And it forfeits the point you were reaching for. 1 Peter 3:15-16 asks for meekness. Colossians 4:6 asks for grace.

The case worth making is about enforcement, not fabric. Wearing is checked through temple-recommend interview questions, and until recently women's garment norms were policed in detail.

That is a question about religious control, and it survives being said respectfully. Ask, do not jeer.

avoid-87-wives-overclaim.responseLead: The documented count is 30 to 40, and the higher tallies pad the list.
avoid-87-wives-overclaim.response:
The documented count is about 30 to 40, and that number is the church's own. The Gospel Topics essay says 'careful estimates put the number between 30 and 40', citing Brian Hales. Todd Compton documents 33.

Higher figures pad the list. Stanley Ivins once tallied 84, using sealings that cannot be verified and sealings performed after Smith's death.

Claiming 87 lets an apologist correct your arithmetic and walk away from the substance.
avoid-87-wives-overclaim.rationaleLead: Do not use this: overclaiming is the one gift you can hand FAIR.
avoid-87-wives-overclaim.rationale:
Overclaiming is the one gift you can give FAIR on this topic. The church-admitted facts need no inflation.

Thirty to forty wives. One aged 14: Helen Mar Kimball, 'sealed months before her 15th birthday', in the essay's own words. Roughly a dozen already married to living husbands. And public denials throughout.

Every clause is sourced to the church's own essay, and covered by this site's other polygamy cases. Say 'thirty to forty, that's your church's number', and nothing can be rebutted.

avoid-mainstream-polygamy-today.responseLead: Since 1904 a plural marriage gets you thrown out. Those pictures are FLDS.
avoid-mainstream-polygamy-today.response:
That is false for the mainstream church.

Since the 1904 Second Manifesto, contracting or performing a plural marriage gets a member excommunicated.

Today's practising polygamists are splinter groups the Latter-day Saint church denounces. The FLDS. The AUB. Various independents.

The prairie-dress image is FLDS, not LDS.
avoid-mainstream-polygamy-today.rationaleLead: Do not use this one. Concede it fast, then ask the question that stands.
avoid-mainstream-polygamy-today.rationale:
Mixing up the Latter-day Saints with the FLDS is the fastest way to be politely dismissed.

But drop the claim about people alive today and the doctrinal one stands untouched. D&C 132 is still canonised scripture. Widowed men are sealed for eternity to more than one wife today, and Presidents Nelson and Oaks each are. And the church's own history has leaders quietly approving plural marriages for fourteen years after the 1890 Manifesto.

Say this. You're right, nobody practises it now. So why is the revelation commanding it still in your scriptures?

avoid-white-horse-prophecy.responseLead: The church repudiated it in 2010, and the text is a 1902 secondhand account.
avoid-white-horse-prophecy.response:
The church officially repudiated it in 2010. Its statement says the story is 'based on accounts that have not been substantiated by historical research and is not embraced as Church doctrine'.

The full White Horse text is a secondhand recollection from 1902, of dubious provenance.

There is a kernel to keep, though. The narrower motif is genuinely and repeatedly attested in leaders' teaching. That the Constitution will hang by a thread, and the elders will save it. Brigham Young and John Taylor taught it, and modern leaders such as Ezra Taft Benson invoked it.
avoid-white-horse-prophecy.rationaleLead: Do not lead with this: use the hang-by-a-thread quotes instead.
avoid-white-horse-prophecy.rationale:
Cite the White Horse document as doctrine and the member quotes the 2010 repudiation back at you. The conversation is over, and you handed them the ending.

The defensible move is the kernel. The hang-by-a-thread teaching came from prophets' own mouths in documented sermons, including Journal of Discourses 7:15.

That raises the same question with sources the church cannot disown as folklore. Use the thread quotes. Never lead with 'White Horse'.

avoid-caffeine-ban.responseLead: Hot drinks means coffee and tea, and BYU has sold caffeinated soda since 2017.
avoid-caffeine-ban.response:
That is false.

The Word of Wisdom's 'hot drinks' at D&C 89:9 has been officially interpreted as coffee and tea only.

The church stated in 2012 that 'the Church does not prohibit the use of caffeine'. BYU has sold caffeinated soda since 2017. Many faithful members drink Coke.

And caffeine appears nowhere in a temple-recommend interview.
avoid-caffeine-ban.rationaleLead: Do not use this as stated: it signals you learned Mormonism from rumour.
avoid-caffeine-ban.rationale:
Getting this wrong signals that you know Mormonism from playground rumour. Everything after it gets discounted.

The incoherence you were reaching for is sharper when stated accurately, and it is already on this site in the Word of Wisdom case. Iced coffee is a temple-worthiness bar, while a quad-shot energy drink is fine. The canonised text calls itself 'not by commandment or constraint' at D&C 89:2, yet became a salvation-gating test decades later. And 'hot drinks' meaning exactly coffee and tea is itself a later reading.

Ask why the line falls where it does. Do not misstate where the line is.

avoid-own-planet.responseLead: The 2014 essay calls that a cartoon, and a church FAQ answers it with no.
avoid-own-planet.response:
The church's 2014 essay pre-loaded the rebuttal. Exaltation, it says, is 'reduced in media to a cartoonish image of people receiving their own planets'. A church FAQ answers the planet question with 'No'.

Say 'own planet' and the member hands you the essay.

The kernel, though, is strong and church-affirmed. Exaltation means becoming gods. D&C 132:20 says 'then shall they be gods', with eternal increase and a share in creation. Past leaders taught it in exactly cosmic terms. Lorenzo Snow. Brigham Young. And Spencer W. Kimball's 'we shall create worlds'.
avoid-own-planet.rationaleLead: Do not use the phrase: the doctrine is conceded, so only the wording is wrong.
avoid-own-planet.rationale:
This is the rare warning case where the doctrine underneath is fully conceded. The error is purely in the packaging.

'Own planet' is South Park vocabulary, and the church has explicitly framed it as caricature. Using it triggers the scripted deflection and skips the real conversation.

Use the member's own words instead. Your scripture says the exalted shall be gods, at D&C 132:20. Isaiah 43:10 says 'before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me'. Can both be true?

The exaltation case on this site carries the full argument.

avoid-1826-convicted-conman.responseLead: It was likely a first hearing, not a trial, and the records do not agree.
avoid-1826-convicted-conman.response:
That is overclaimed.

The 1826 Bainbridge proceeding was real. Smith, aged 20, was charged as a 'disorderly person' over paid 'glass looking'. Justice Neely's own fee bill labels him 'The Glass Looker'.

But it was likely a preliminary examination. The surviving records are fragmentary and they contradict each other. The Pearsall account says 'guilty', while the fee bill and mittimus evidence point the other way.

Scholars dispute the outcome. Gordon Madsen reads an acquittal or discharge. Dan Vogel and Wesley Walters disagree. So 'convicted of fraud' states as fact what the documents cannot establish.
avoid-1826-convicted-conman.rationaleLead: Never say convicted: lead with the seer stone the church itself admits.
avoid-1826-convicted-conman.rationale: Say 'convicted' and the apologist wins the exchange on the record's ambiguity. And that ambiguity is genuine, not spin. Here is the core that needs no conviction. By the church's own Gospel Topics admission, and by Richard Bushman in Rough Stone Rolling, Smith was a paid treasure-seer. He hunted buried valuables by staring at a stone in his hat. It was the same stone, in the same hat, that he then used to produce the Book of Mormon. The 1826 court documents back up that occupation whatever the verdict. Lead with the church-admitted seer-stone facts, and let the 1826 record confirm the timeline.
